items.title: Implement native endpoint failure policies and wire encryption
items.body:
Implement ordered typed/predicate failure policies, immediate/cooldown/requeue/scheduled/discard/dead-letter/pause actions, receive/send circuit rules and bounded terminal fault contracts. Integrate rather than silently retry side effects. Add opt-in authenticated AES-256-GCM message encryption with key-provider rotation/selection, receive enforcement and tamper/known-answer cases. Preserve tenant/ordering/failure boundaries.

Acceptance:
- [ ] Map the relevant Wolverine V6.62.0 behavior rows to explicit Rust-native contracts without dropping clauses.
- [ ] Implement the behavior with bounded typed APIs, real integration and documented failure/cancellation/ownership semantics.
- [ ] Verify valid work before/after first/middle/last failures, corrected retries, crashes and unknown outcomes as applicable.
- [ ] Independently review and qualify the exact integrated head before closing any supported parity rows.

Part of #34. No copied upstream implementation, new CI pipelines, unapproved cloud entities or proprietary EULA acceptance.

items.title: Backend and the shared schema library have diverged; the backend does not consume it
items.body:
Audit finding from 2026-08-11, logged while cleaning up packaging in the shared library. **No code was changed and nothing is currently broken** — the backend works correctly on its own schemas. This is architectural drift to resolve deliberately.

## Current state

The backend declares the shared schema library as a dependency in one of its two dependency manifests, but the manifest that is actually installed does not list it, and there are **zero imports** of it anywhere in the backend. The declared dependency is inert; the backend runs entirely on its own schema definitions.

## Where the two sides diverged

Verified by reading both definitions:

| Symbol | shared library | backend | Conflict |
|---|---|---|---|
| curation status enum | `accept` / `review` / `reject` (3 values) | `pending` / `accepted` / `review` / `rejected` / `manual_accepted` / `manual_rejected` (6) | every wire value differs — `accept` is not `accepted` |
| quality score | requires an overall score plus a quality level | requires a differently-named overall field, no quality level | mutually unsatisfiable (see #14 in the backend tracker for the related field retirement) |
| search metadata | tags are a nested structured object | tags are a flat list of strings | type conflict |
| EXIF | single camera field, one timestamp field, short GPS field names | split make/model, differently-named date and GPS fields, plus pixel dimensions | different field names for the same data |

## Part of this divergence is deliberate and should be preserved

The two libraries model **different contracts**. The shared library describes the stored record as the ML pipeline writes it. The backend describes the HTTP response the frontend consumes.

The backend's EXIF construction already reads *both* spellings on purpose, with a comment noting field names are writer-dependent, and it deliberately omits the image embedding from responses because it would add roughly 15KB per image to list payloads with no client use.

**Adopting the shared schemas wholesale would be a regression.** Any future work should keep the backend's schema layer as the API contract boundary.

## The safe win is constants, not schemas

The backend duplicates the supported-format list — 34 extensions — and it is **currently byte-identical** to the shared library's copy (diffed programmatically; zero difference in either direction). The backend's own comment above that list says it must match the frontend's list exactly.

That is a hand-maintained three-way sync across backend, frontend, and the shared library. It matches today by discipline, not by construction — precisely the failure mode a shared library exists to remove.

Environment-specific resource names and the deployment region are likewise hardcoded in backend config rather than derived from the shared naming templates.

## Blocker to resolve first

The shared library is **not published to any package index**, and the backend has no private index configured. The ML service obtains it through a sibling source checkout installed directly. Wiring it into the backend requires deciding an install story *before* any code change.

## Scope when picked up

- [ ] Decide the install story for the shared library in the backend
- [ ] Import the supported-format set and resource-name templates from shared; drop the local copies
- [ ] Leave the backend schema layer alone as the API contract
- [ ] Collapse a duplicated curation status enum that exists twice inside the backend

items.body:
<!-- planning-id: M16-01 -->

**Milestone:** M16 — Observability, Security & Resilience Hardening  
**Planning ID:** `M16-01`  
**Size:** L (planning estimate)  
**Requirements/traceability:** FR-PLT-03

## Summary
Operating the platform requires logs, metrics and traces with correlation across services.

## Dependencies
Blocked by:
- #43 — kafka-client v2: supervised consumer runner with retries and DLQ
- #99 — Payment-intent webhook processing with ledger posting

Do not start until the issues above are merged. If a dependency is missing, comment and stop.

## Current state
Pino logger preset (`packages/logger`) exists; services mostly log via `console.log`; no metrics or tracing.

## Expected behavior
Record the observability tooling choice in the PR (default proposal: a free-tier log/metrics backend plus error tracking; no paid plan without approval); platform log streaming from each service; `@betterbasket/runtime` instruments RED metrics per route and client timings for DB/Kafka/Stripe/inter-service calls; business metrics (orders created/paid/cancelled, checkout failures by reason, reservation conflicts/expiries, transfers pending/failed, DLQ depth, outbox oldest age, consumer lag, reconciliation exceptions, seller-access latency); W3C `traceparent` propagated gateway → services → outbox headers → consumers; dashboards exported as files under `ops/dashboards/` *(new)* per environment.

## Technical approach and files
OpenTelemetry SDK (or Prometheus-format endpoint) behind a small interface in `packages/runtime`.

## Implementation steps
1. Tooling decision + free-tier limit check.
2. Instrumentation library.
3. Business metrics.
4. Trace propagation.
5. Dashboards.

## API / data / event / UI changes
none (telemetry only).

## Security, authorization and tenant isolation
No PII/secrets in telemetry; sampling configured (10%, 100% on errors).

## Error handling, edge cases and recovery
Backend unavailable (drop with a counter, never block requests); cardinality control for labels.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Given one staging checkout, then a single trace spans gateway → order → product → outbox → consumer
- [ ] Given dashboards, then the listed business metrics are visible.

## Testing requirements
Instrumentation unit tests; staging verification.

## Documentation updates
`infra/README.md` observability section.

_Update in-repository files listed here. Maintainer-held design documents live outside this repository; if you cannot see them, list the required changes in the pull request description._

## Definition of done
Standard DoD; usage within free limits documented. (see "Reference: dod-standard" below for the standard checklist).

## Out of scope
Paid plans.

## Embedded references
Essential constraints are inlined below so this issue is self-contained.

<details>
<summary>Reference: repo-context</summary>

**Repository:** pnpm 10 + Turborepo monorepo, Node 22, TypeScript. Apps (`apps/`): NestJS services `gateway` (4000), `auth-service` (4001), `product-service` (4002), `seller-service` (4003), `order-service` (4004), `payment-service` (4005), `notification-service` (4006), `media-service` (4007), `analytics-service` (4008); Next.js 15 apps `web` (3000), `seller-portal` (3001), `admin-portal` (3002). Shared packages (`packages/`): `contracts` (Zod schemas for DTOs/events), `auth-shared` (JWT/JWKS verification, guards), `kafka-client`, `logger` (Pino), `utils`, `ui`, `config` (eslint/tsconfig). Postgres (Drizzle) for auth/seller/order/payment; MongoDB (Mongoose) for product; Redis for rate limits/cache; Kafka-compatible broker for events. All datastores are managed cloud services — **no local Docker is required or may be introduced as a dependency**. Commands: `pnpm install`, `pnpm turbo run lint type-check test build --filter=<pkg>...`, `pnpm --filter <app> <script>`. Each service validates DTOs with Zod from `@betterbasket/contracts` (not class-validator) and exposes `GET /health`. Services compile to CommonJS.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Reference: nfr-targets</summary>

Provisional initial targets (not commitments): checkout-path availability 99.5%/month; `GET /products` p95 ≤400 ms (p99 ≤1 s); product detail p95 ≤300 ms; `POST /orders` p95 ≤1.5 s; `POST /payments/intents` p95 ≤1.5 s; sign-in p95 ≤800 ms; order becomes `paid` ≤10 s p95 after Stripe success; outbox publish p95 ≤2 s; event end-to-end p95 ≤5 s; transactional email p95 ≤60 s; 5xx ≤0.5%; DLQ ≤0.1% of events; realtime delivery p95 ≤2 s; Core Web Vitals p75 LCP ≤2.5 s, INP ≤200 ms, CLS ≤0.1. Launch capacity assumption: 100 concurrent users, 5 orders/min peak, ≤10,000 products.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Reference: cost-gate</summary>

Do not create, upgrade or enable any paid cloud resource, subscription or add-on as part of this issue unless a written cost proposal (resources, expected monthly cost, alternatives) has been approved by the maintainer in this issue or its milestone. Prefer free tiers, trials and usage-based resources; provision incrementally; clean up temporary resources after spikes and record evidence.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Reference: security-baseline</summary>

Validate all input with strict Zod schemas; enforce authorization and tenant scoping on the server for every route; return 404 for foreign objects; never log secrets, tokens, card data, full emails/addresses; parameterized queries only (Drizzle; Mongo filters built from allow-listed fields, never from raw client operators); rate limit abuse-prone endpoints; use constant-time comparison for secrets/signatures; secrets only from validated environment configuration (service fails to start if a required secret is missing; no placeholder defaults); dependencies pinned via lockfile; add negative tests for each authorization rule introduced.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Reference: dod-standard</summary>

Implementation matches *Expected behavior*; every acceptance criterion passes with automated evidence; required tests added and green in CI (no skipped tests without a linked issue); lint, type-check, build, contract and migration checks pass; docs updated; security requirements satisfied including negative/authorization tests; no secrets, credentials or real customer/payment data in code, fixtures, logs or PR text; PR description complete; deployment verification performed when the issue affects a deployed environment.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Reference: agent-workflow</summary>

1. Read this whole issue; inspect the files named under *Technical approach*; confirm every item under *Current state* is still true (the codebase may have moved). 2. Verify each dependency issue is merged (see *Dependencies*); if a prerequisite is missing, stop and comment — do not re-implement it. 3. Post a short implementation plan as a comment before large changes. 4. Implement exactly the *Expected behavior*; respect *Out of scope*. 5. Write the tests listed under *Tests* (unit, integration, contract, E2E as applicable); run lint, type-check, tests and build for every touched package. 6. Review your own diff for security issues (authorization, tenant scoping, input validation, secret handling, logging of sensitive data) and regressions. 7. Update documentation named under *Docs* (in-repo files; if the maintainer's private design docs exist locally, update the affected sections too, otherwise list the required changes in the PR). 8. Check every acceptance criterion and quote the evidence (test names/output) in the PR description. 9. Open a reviewable PR: link this issue, list requirements covered, architectural impact, tests added, docs updated, migration/deployment impact. 10. If blocked or if a decision is unresolved, stop, comment with the question and options, and apply the `blocked:decision` label — do not guess or make architectural decisions that are not in this issue.

</details>

items.title: Multi-tenant data isolation

milestone.title: Later
milestone.description: Unscheduled. Pulled into an R milestone when a customer or a regulation needs it. Holds the open remainder of M0-M2, M6-M9 and MVP 1 (MVP 1 items keep the release:MVP 1 label).

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Situation

The platform will hold patient records, prescriptions, lab results and pharmacy dispensing history for many unrelated hospitals, laboratories and pharmacies in the same PostgreSQL 16 cluster. Today there is no isolation mechanism at all: any handler that forgets a `WHERE tenant_id = ?` clause would return another hospital's patients. In healthcare that is not a bug, it is a reportable data breach — under the **DPDP Act 2023** the platform, acting as Data Processor, would have to notify the affected Data Fiduciaries and the Data Protection Board, and under **CERT-In** directions the incident must be reported within the mandated window with retained logs to support the investigation.

Relying on developer discipline is not a control. Across eleven products and hundreds of endpoints, a single missed predicate in a reporting query, an admin export, a background reconciliation job or a `Raw()` GORM call is enough. The affected parties are every patient on the platform, every hospital admin whose accreditation (**NABH**) and every laboratory whose **NABL** status depends on demonstrable confidentiality controls, and the DPO who must be able to state, with evidence, that cross-tenant access is structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely.

There is a second dimension: some enterprise hospital groups will contractually require physical separation and will not accept a shared schema. The isolation design must therefore support shared-schema row-level security as the default and schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant as premium tiers, without every module knowing which mode it is running in.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** platform engineer building any HMS module
**I want** tenant isolation enforced by the database and a single tenant-scoped data-access layer rather than by per-query discipline
**So that** no application code path — including reports, exports, background jobs and ad-hoc queries — can read or write another tenant's data even if the developer forgets.

### Scope

**In scope**

* PostgreSQL row-level security enabled and forced on every tenant-owned table, with `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` policies bound to a session-scoped tenant setting.
* A single tenant-scoped data-access layer in Go that acquires a connection, sets the tenant context inside the transaction, and is the only supported way to obtain a `*gorm.DB`.
* Gin middleware that resolves the tenant from the authenticated principal's claims (never from a client-supplied header) and fails closed when absent.
* A migration lint that fails CI if a new table carrying a `tenant_id` column ships without RLS enabled, forced and policied.
* Object-storage isolation: per-tenant key prefixes and signed URLs scoped to that prefix with a short expiry.
* Isolation mode abstraction so `shared_rls`, `schema` and `database` modes are resolved by connection routing without module-level branching.
* An adversarial cross-tenant test suite executed in CI: for every read and write endpoint, attempt access with a valid token from tenant B against tenant A's resource identifiers.
* NATS JetStream subject and consumer naming that carries the tenant so no subscriber receives another tenant's events.
* Per-tenant connection-pool and query cost limits to contain noisy neighbours.

**Out of scope**

* The tenant registry and lifecycle itself — owned by *Tenant management* (#13).
* Per-tenant encryption keys, isolated backup streams and export controls — tracked separately in the Data Isolation epic.
* Country-level residency partitioning and regional deployment topology — a separate infrastructure decision above tenancy.
* Relationship-based clinical authorisation (which clinician may see which patient *within* a tenant) — owned by the OpenFGA care-relationship model.
* Analytics/OLAP isolation; the warehouse holds de-identified aggregates only and is governed by its own epic.

---

## Recommended Solution

Treat the database as the enforcement point and the data-access layer as the only gate, then prove it adversarially.

### Row-level security

Every tenant-owned table carries a non-null `tenant_id uuid REFERENCES tenant(id)`. Applications connect as a role that is **not** the table owner and does **not** hold `BYPASSRLS`:

```sql
ALTER TABLE patient ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE patient FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY patient_tenant_read ON patient FOR SELECT
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('hms.tenant_id', true)::uuid);

CREATE POLICY patient_tenant_write ON patient FOR ALL
  USING      (tenant_id = current_setting('hms.tenant_id', true)::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('hms.tenant_id', true)::uuid);
```

The `WITH CHECK` clause is essential — without it a tenant could insert or update a row *into* another tenant. `current_setting(..., true)` returning NULL evaluates the predicate to NULL, which denies rather than permits, so an unset context fails closed.

### Tenant-scoped data-access layer

```go
// The only way to obtain a handle. No exported *gorm.DB elsewhere.
func (r *Runtime) WithTenant(ctx context.Context, fn func(tx *gorm.DB) error) error {
    tid, ok := tenantctx.From(ctx)
    if !ok { return ErrNoTenantContext }
    return r.route(tid).Transaction(func(tx *gorm.DB) error {
        if err := tx.Exec("SELECT set_config('hms.tenant_id', ?, true)", tid).Error; err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return fn(tx)
    })
}
```

`set_config(..., true)` scopes the setting to the transaction, so a pooled connection returned to PgBouncer cannot leak context into the next request. `route(tid)` resolves the isolation mode from a Redis-cached tenant descriptor and returns the shared pool, a schema-qualified pool, or a dedicated pool — the only place isolation mode is known.

A `go vet`-style custom analyser plus an architecture test fail the build if any package outside the runtime imports `gorm.io/gorm` and constructs a session directly, or calls `Raw`/`Exec` outside `WithTenant`.

### Tenant resolution

Gin middleware reads the `tenant_id` claim from the Keycloak-issued token, cross-checks it against the OpenFGA `can_access` relation for the requested tenant object, and injects it into the context. A `X-Tenant-Id` request header is accepted only for platform operators holding `operator` on `platform`, and that path is separately audited.

```
type tenant
  relations
    define member: [user, service_account]
    define admin: [user]
    define can_access: member or admin or operator from platform
```

### Adversarial testing

A table-driven suite enumerates the OpenAPI surface, seeds two tenants with identical-shaped fixtures, and for each operation issues tenant B's token against tenant A's resource id. Anything other than 403/404 fails the build. A second suite runs raw SQL as the application role with `hms.tenant_id` unset and asserts zero rows from every RLS-protected table. Both run in CI on every pull request and nightly against a synthetic-data environment; PHI never appears in non-production.

### Events and storage

JetStream subjects are `hms.{country}.{tenant_id}.{domain}.{event}` with durable consumers filtered by tenant, so a misconfigured subscriber cannot wildcard across tenants. Object keys are `{tenant_id}/{domain}/{object_id}`; signed URLs are minted only by the storage service after an OpenFGA check and expire in 15 minutes.

### Sequencing and risks

Depends on #13 for `tenant.id` and on Keycloak claim mapping. The main risks are: a superuser or migration role bypassing RLS — mitigated by `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` and a separate, non-owning application role; connection pooling leaking context — mitigated by transaction-local `set_config` and a pool test that interleaves two tenants on one connection; and RLS predicate cost on large tables — mitigated by composite indexes leading with `tenant_id` and a query-plan regression check on the highest-traffic clinical reads.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** two active tenants, a ward nurse authenticated against tenant A, and patient records existing in both
**When** the nurse lists patients through any MediCore endpoint
**Then** only tenant A's records are returned, the executed statement carries `hms.tenant_id` set to tenant A inside the transaction, and the same query run without that setting returns zero rows.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** a valid, unexpired token issued to a pathologist in tenant B
**When** that token is used to request a diagnostic report belonging to tenant A by its exact identifier
**Then** the request is rejected with 404 (not 403, to avoid confirming existence), no row is returned, the RLS policy denies at the database layer even if the handler's predicate were removed, and an audit record of the attempted cross-tenant access is written with the principal, tenant pair and resource type.

### Edge Cases

* A background reconciliation job runs with no HTTP request context — it must enumerate tenants explicitly and open one `WithTenant` scope per tenant; an unscoped run fails fast rather than reading everything.
* A connection is returned to the pool mid-request and reused by another tenant — transaction-local settings must prevent any bleed; covered by an interleaved-connection test.
* A new table is added in a migration with a `tenant_id` column but no policy — CI migration lint fails the pull request.
* A tenant in `database` isolation mode is queried through the shared pool — the router must refuse rather than silently fall back to shared RLS.
* A signed object-storage URL for tenant A is replayed by a user in tenant B before expiry — the storage service re-checks the prefix and rejects.
* A JetStream consumer is created with a wildcard subject spanning tenants — rejected by the consumer-provisioning helper.

---

## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** cross-tenant data access is structurally impossible; a forgotten predicate produces zero rows rather than another hospital's patients.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** the platform can evidence its confidentiality controls to hospital procurement, NABH and NABL assessors, and to enterprise groups evaluating the premium isolation tiers.
* **Success metric or validation method:** 100% of tenant-owned tables have RLS enabled and forced, verified by an automated catalogue assertion; the adversarial suite covers at least 95% of authenticated endpoints with zero cross-tenant successes; p95 latency on the top ten clinical read queries increases by no more than 5% against the pre-RLS baseline.
* **Monitoring period:** continuous — the catalogue assertion and adversarial suite run nightly; a 30-day latency watch follows the first production rollout.

---

## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team’s agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
* [ ] Existing tests pass.
* [ ] No new flaky or skipped tests are introduced without justification.

### Security and Access

* [ ] Authentication and authorisation are enforced at the appropriate layer.
* [ ] Users and services can access only the data and actions they require.
* [ ] Input is validated and sensitive information is not exposed in logs or errors.
* [ ] Secrets and credentials are not stored in source code.
* [ ] Security and dependency scans pass.
* [ ] Tenant, account or customer isolation is tested where applicable.

### Accessibility and User Journey

* [ ] The primary user journey works from start to completion.
* [ ] Loading, empty, success and error states are handled.
* [ ] Keyboard navigation and focus behaviour work correctly.
* [ ] Controls have clear labels and accessible names.
* [ ] The change meets the team’s agreed WCAG accessibility level.
* [ ] The experience works across supported devices and browsers.

### Performance and Reliability

* [ ] The change does not introduce unnecessary API calls, database queries or processing.
* [ ] Timeouts, retries and failure behaviour are defined where applicable.
* [ ] Duplicate requests do not create inconsistent data.
* [ ] Performance-sensitive changes are tested against an agreed threshold.
* [ ] Partial failures do not leave the system in an invalid state.

### Observability

* [ ] Important failures are logged with useful diagnostic context.
* [ ] Logs do not contain sensitive information.
* [ ] Metrics or traces are added where the change affects a critical workflow.
* [ ] The team can determine whether the feature is working correctly after deployment.

### Documentation

* [ ] Relevant README, API or technical documentation is updated.
* [ ] Configuration or environment changes are documented.
* [ ] Deployment, migration or rollback steps are documented where required.
* [ ] Known limitations are recorded.

---

## Pull Request Evidence

The pull request should include:

* [ ] Link to this story.
* [ ] Summary of the change.
* [ ] Test evidence.
* [ ] Screenshots or recordings for UI changes.
* [ ] Security, accessibility or performance evidence where relevant.
* [ ] Deployment and rollback notes for higher-risk changes.
* [ ] Known risks or follow-up work.

---

## Definition of Done

The story is complete when:

* [ ] All acceptance criteria pass.
* [ ] Required tests pass locally and in CI.
* [ ] No critical or high-severity security or quality issues remain.
* [ ] The critical user or system journey has been validated.
* [ ] Documentation is updated.
* [ ] Code review is complete.
* [ ] The change has been deployed or is ready for deployment through the standard pipeline.
* [ ] Post-deployment validation is defined or completed.
* [ ] Any exception is documented with an owner and reason.

---

## Exceptions

**Guardrail:** Accessibility and User Journey — keyboard navigation, accessible names, WCAG level, cross-device behaviour.
**Reason:** This story delivers database policies, a Go data-access runtime, Gin middleware and CI checks. It ships no user interface. The only user-visible effect is that out-of-tenant resources return 404, which is rendered by the already-accessible shared design-system error state owned by the console epic.
**Alternative validation:** The Playwright journey suite is run unchanged before and after the RLS rollout to confirm no existing accessible journey regresses, and the "resource not found" state is verified against the design-system component's existing accessibility tests.
**Residual risk:** Low. A latency regression from RLS predicates could degrade perceived responsiveness on slower Android devices; covered by the p95 threshold in the Result section rather than by an accessibility check.
**Approved by:** Platform Team lead (to confirm at review).

items.title: Epic: Evidence-grounded memory pipeline and maintained project briefs
items.body:
## Goal

Turn the Hindsight research into a measured, evidence-grounded Continuum roadmap without replacing Continuum's stronger lifecycle/security model or duplicating Engram's code intelligence.

Source: [Hindsight research report](https://github.com/nucleoid/openclaw-workspace/blob/main/second-brain/projects/hindsight-continuum-research-2026-10-16.md), based on `vectorize-io/hindsight@9a499b1759084a86598eff8af30ed59f7354e76c` and Continuum baseline `51fe3a8b9a133fac1969e282fcc08a3aadd96525`.

## Architecture boundary

- **Engram owns code-only architecture intelligence:** implemented symbols, flows, dependencies, contracts, and change impact.
- **Continuum owns memory semantics:** decisions, rationale, constraints, rejected alternatives, supersession, provenance, authorization, and lifecycle.
- Maintained project briefs are thin, source-neutral synthesis over authorized evidence. They distinguish implemented facts, recorded intent, and inference; cite source-memory versions and repository commit/index freshness; surface contradictions; and invalidate/refresh affected sections.
- Engram is optional. Continuum keeps full non-code utility. No Engram API is assumed.
- Continuum scope authorization never grants repository evidence access. Every stage requires the intersection of caller authority, source/assertion authority, connector authority, and residency/provider policy.

## Child work (dependency order)

- [ ] #25 — evaluation corpus and ablation harness
- [ ] #26 — assertion/source authorization and threat model (depends on #25)
- [ ] #27 — versioned evidence DAG, quarantine, and erasure (depends on #26)
- [ ] #28 — serialized context/output/deadline/spend budgets (depends on #25, #26)
- [ ] #29 — pre-final-cut reranking (depends on #25, #26, #28)
- [ ] #30 — optional source-preserving extraction (depends on #25–#28)
- [ ] #31 — event time, ingestion time, TTL, hard filters, and ranking hints (depends on #25, #27)
- [ ] #32 — optional source-neutral Engram connector/query receipts (depends on #26–#28)
- [ ] #33 — scoped maintained briefs (depends on #25–#31; #32 optional)
- [ ] #34 — bounded typed relationship expansion, only if measured (depends on #25–#29 foundations)

## Cross-cutting acceptance criteria

- Evaluation covers retrieval, extraction, synthesis, security, temporal/supersession/deletion behavior, latency, and spend with ablations and frozen fixtures.
- Persistent derivatives use versioned evidence dependencies and are synchronously quarantined after source deletion, revocation, or material change; asynchronous repair never leaves stale prose readable.
- Source-document and extracted-assertion authorization remain separate through extraction, reranking, source expansion, synthesis, cache/history/export, and optional connectors.
- Prompt injection and untrusted-source threats, repeated-source non-independence, failures/fallbacks, provider/local-only controls, resource ceilings, audit, Entra/ACL/offboarding, and erasure are explicit.
- Explicit decision supersession remains authoritative. Deterministic `AGENTS.md` output remains a separate trustworthy reference, not an LLM-maintained brief.

## Non-goals

- Replacing Continuum with Hindsight or adopting Hindsight as a backend.
- Making personality/agent dispositions the default memory model.
- Prompt-based declassification, tags as an ACL substitute, or proof count as truth probability.
- Duplicating Engram's code graph or inventing Engram APIs.
- Building a general relationship graph before measured benefit.
- Deployment, migration, infrastructure changes, or production rollout under this planning epic.

Related existing delivery work: #18, #19, #20, #21. Those issues cover transport, packaging, deployment, and UAT rather than this memory-architecture roadmap.

items.body:
## Situation

The platform has no tenant registry. There is currently no record that a given hospital, laboratory, pharmacy or warehouse exists, which country profile governs it, which subscription tier it holds, or whether it is live, in trial, suspended for non-payment or being offboarded. Every other foundational capability depends on this: row-level security has no `tenant_id` to bind to, the country-profile rules engine has no country to resolve, entitlement checks have nothing to look up, and billing has no legal entity to raise a GST invoice against.

Without it, onboarding a hospital would mean an engineer running SQL by hand against production — unauditable, error-prone, and unacceptable for a system holding patient data. Platform operations cannot suspend a defaulting tenant, cannot see how many facilities are live, and cannot prove to an auditor when a tenant's data processing began or ended.

This is legally load-bearing, not merely operational. Under the **DPDP Act 2023** each tenant is a Data Fiduciary in its own right and the platform is a Data Processor acting under a data processing agreement; the tenant record is where that relationship, its start date, its termination date and the nominated Grievance Officer are held. **GST** requires a GSTIN and place-of-supply per legal entity for correct invoicing and for e-invoicing above the notified turnover threshold. Data residency obligations mean a tenant must be pinned to a country and its regional deployment at creation and must never silently move.

Affected roles: platform operations (creates and suspends tenants), hospital admin (receives a working workspace on day one), finance (invoicing), and the DPO (needs a defensible record of every processing relationship).

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** platform operations engineer in AdminConnect
**I want** to create, configure, activate, suspend and offboard a tenant through an audited, workflow-driven lifecycle
**So that** every hospital, lab, pharmacy or warehouse on the platform has a single authoritative record that governs its isolation, entitlements, country behaviour and billing.

### Scope

**In scope**

* A `tenant` aggregate holding legal name, trading name, tenant type, country profile code, residency region, subscription tier, isolation mode and lifecycle state.
* An explicit lifecycle state machine — `draft → provisioning → trial → active → suspended → offboarding → offboarded` — with only legal transitions permitted and every transition recorded with actor, reason and timestamp.
* A Temporal-orchestrated provisioning workflow that creates the Keycloak realm mapping, seeds the OpenFGA tenant object and initial admin relation, creates object-storage prefixes, applies default configuration and emits `TenantCreated`/`TenantActivated`.
* Idempotent creation keyed on an operator-supplied idempotency key so a retried request cannot produce two tenants.
* Suspension semantics: authentication continues but write operations are rejected with a machine-readable reason; EmergencyConnect remains available where a suspended tenant has active ambulance jobs.
* Legal-entity and tax attributes: GSTIN, PAN, registered address, place-of-supply state code, nominated Grievance Officer contact.
* AdminConnect console screens for the tenant list, tenant detail and lifecycle actions, with a typed reason required for suspension and offboarding.
* OpenTelemetry spans and metrics covering provisioning duration and failure rate.

**Out of scope**

* Row-level security enforcement and the tenant-scoped data-access layer — owned by *Multi-tenant data isolation* (#14).
* The tenant-type-specific attribute sets and their validation (hospital, laboratory, pharmacy, warehouse) — owned by #15–#20.
* Subscription plans, entitlement evaluation and metered billing — owned by the Subscriptions & Entitlements epic.
* Country-profile authoring and the regulatory rules engine itself; this story only stores and resolves the profile code.
* Tenant branding, theming and custom domains.

---

## Recommended Solution

Build tenant management as a control-plane module in the Go 1.26 modular monolith (`internal/adminconnect/tenancy`), Gin handlers over a GORM repository, backed by PostgreSQL 16. The control plane is deliberately separate from the per-country clinical data stores: it holds tenant metadata, billing metadata and feature configuration only, never PHI, so it can be queried globally without breaching residency.

### Data model

```sql
CREATE TABLE tenant (
  id                uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  slug              citext NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  legal_name        text NOT NULL,
  trading_name      text,
  tenant_type       text NOT NULL,   -- healthcare_org | hospital_group | hospital | clinic |
                                     -- laboratory | pharmacy | warehouse | ambulance_provider
  parent_tenant_id  uuid REFERENCES tenant(id),
  country_profile   text NOT NULL,   -- 'IN' today; NP/AF later
  residency_region  text NOT NULL,   -- e.g. asia-south1; immutable after activation
  isolation_mode    text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'shared_rls',  -- shared_rls | schema | database
  lifecycle_state   text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'draft',
  gstin             text, pan text, place_of_supply text,
  grievance_officer jsonb,
  activated_at      timestamptz, suspended_at timestamptz, offboarded_at timestamptz,
  created_at        timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  version           bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  CONSTRAINT gstin_fmt CHECK (gstin IS NULL OR gstin ~ '^[0-9]{2}[A-Z0-9]{13}$')
);
CREATE TABLE tenant_lifecycle_event (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tenant(id),
  from_state text, to_state text NOT NULL, reason_code text NOT NULL,
  reason_note text, actor_subject text NOT NULL, occurred_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  prev_hash bytea, hash bytea NOT NULL   -- tamper-evident chain
);
CREATE TABLE tenant_provisioning_run (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id uuid NOT NULL, workflow_id text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  status text NOT NULL, failed_step text, last_error text, started_at timestamptz, finished_at timestamptz
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX tenant_idem ON tenant_creation_request (idempotency_key);
```

`residency_region` and `country_profile` are immutable once `lifecycle_state` reaches `active`, enforced by a database trigger as well as in the domain layer — a mistake here would move PHI across a hard residency boundary.

### API surface

| Method | Path | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| POST | `/admin/v1/tenants` | Create in `draft`; requires `Idempotency-Key` |
| GET | `/admin/v1/tenants` | Filter by type, state, country, tier |
| GET | `/admin/v1/tenants/{id}` | Detail including current provisioning run |
| PATCH | `/admin/v1/tenants/{id}` | Mutable attributes only |
| POST | `/admin/v1/tenants/{id}:provision` | Start `TenantProvisioningWorkflow` |
| POST | `/admin/v1/tenants/{id}:activate` | Trial or active |
| POST | `/admin/v1/tenants/{id}:suspend` | Requires `reason_code` |
| POST | `/admin/v1/tenants/{id}:resume` | |
| POST | `/admin/v1/tenants/{id}:offboard` | Starts retention-and-export workflow |
| GET | `/admin/v1/tenants/{id}/lifecycle-events` | Audit trail |

### Orchestration and events

`TenantProvisioningWorkflow` (Temporal) runs activities in order: reserve slug → create Keycloak realm/client mapping → write OpenFGA tenant object and `admin` relation for the nominated hospital admin → create object-storage prefix `s3://hms-{region}/{tenant_id}/` → seed default configuration from the country profile → emit events. Every activity is idempotent and the workflow compensates on permanent failure by marking the tenant `draft` with `failed_step` set, so a half-provisioned tenant is never left `active`.

Events published to NATS JetStream on `platform.tenant.*`: `TenantCreated`, `TenantProvisioned`, `TenantActivated`, `TenantSuspended`, `TenantResumed`, `TenantOffboarded`. Downstream modules (LabConnect, PharmaConnect, SupplyConnect, billing, analytics) subscribe rather than reading the tenant table directly.

```json
{ "event": "TenantSuspended", "tenant_id": "…", "reason_code": "PAYMENT_OVERDUE",
  "effective_at": "2026-08-01T00:00:00Z", "emergency_grace": true, "version": 1 }
```

### Authorisation

Control-plane operations are authorised in OpenFGA against a `platform` object, not the tenant itself, so a hospital admin can never suspend or reconfigure their own tenant:

```
type platform
  relations
    define operator: [user]
    define auditor: [user]
type tenant
  relations
    define parent: [tenant]
    define admin: [user] or admin from parent
    define managed_by: [user] from operator of platform
    define can_suspend: managed_by
    define can_view: admin or managed_by or auditor from platform
```

### Sequencing and risks

Depends on Keycloak realm provisioning and the OpenFGA store being available; #14 depends on this landing first because RLS binds to `tenant.id`. Principal risks: a partially provisioned tenant appearing usable — mitigated by the workflow-driven state machine and the rule that only `TenantProvisioned` may promote to `trial`; and residency drift — mitigated by immutability triggers plus an integration test asserting an update attempt is rejected.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** a platform operator with the `operator` relation on `platform`
**When** they create a tenant of type `hospital` with country profile `IN`, residency `asia-south1` and a valid GSTIN, then trigger provisioning
**Then** a `TenantProvisioningWorkflow` completes, the tenant reaches `trial`, `TenantCreated` and `TenantProvisioned` are published, the nominated hospital admin holds the `admin` relation in OpenFGA, and the lifecycle trail shows both transitions with the operator's subject.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** the OpenFGA store is unreachable during provisioning
**When** the relationship-seeding activity is retried to its retry limit
**Then** the workflow fails without compensating side effects being left behind, the tenant remains in `draft` with `failed_step = "seed_openfga"`, no `TenantProvisioned` event is published, no user can sign in to the tenant, and the failure is surfaced on the AdminConnect tenant detail screen with a retry action.

### Edge Cases

* The same `Idempotency-Key` is replayed after a network timeout — the original tenant is returned with HTTP 200, not a duplicate created.
* An operator attempts to change `residency_region` on an `active` tenant — rejected by both the domain layer and the database trigger.
* A hospital admin calls `:suspend` on their own tenant — rejected with 403 and no lifecycle event written.
* A suspended tenant's ambulance crew has an in-flight EmergencyConnect job — dispatch and handover continue; only non-emergency writes are blocked.
* Slug collision on creation — rejected with a 409 naming the conflicting field, before any workflow starts.
* Offboarding is requested while a provisioning workflow is still running — rejected until the run terminates.

---

## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** platform operations can stand up a fully isolated, correctly configured tenant from the AdminConnect console without engineering involvement, and can suspend or offboard one with a complete audit trail.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** hospital onboarding stops being a manual engineering task; suspension for non-payment becomes a supported, same-day operation.
* **Success metric or validation method:** provisioning completes end to end in under 90 seconds at p95, with a provisioning success rate above 99% over a rolling 30 days; zero tenants observed in `active` without a completed provisioning run; 100% of lifecycle transitions carry an actor and reason code.
* **Monitoring period:** 30 days after the first production tenant, tracking `tenant_provisioning_duration_seconds` and `tenant_provisioning_failures_total` in the OpenTelemetry pipeline.

---

## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team’s agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
* [ ] Existing tests pass.
* [ ] No new flaky or skipped tests are introduced without justification.

### Security and Access

* [ ] Authentication and authorisation are enforced at the appropriate layer.
* [ ] Users and services can access only the data and actions they require.
* [ ] Input is validated and sensitive information is not exposed in logs or errors.
* [ ] Secrets and credentials are not stored in source code.
* [ ] Security and dependency scans pass.
* [ ] Tenant, account or customer isolation is tested where applicable.

### Accessibility and User Journey

* [ ] The primary user journey works from start to completion.
* [ ] Loading, empty, success and error states are handled.
* [ ] Keyboard navigation and focus behaviour work correctly.
* [ ] Controls have clear labels and accessible names.
* [ ] The change meets the team’s agreed WCAG accessibility level.
* [ ] The experience works across supported devices and browsers.

### Performance and Reliability

* [ ] The change does not introduce unnecessary API calls, database queries or processing.
* [ ] Timeouts, retries and failure behaviour are defined where applicable.
* [ ] Duplicate requests do not create inconsistent data.
* [ ] Performance-sensitive changes are tested against an agreed threshold.
* [ ] Partial failures do not leave the system in an invalid state.

### Observability

* [ ] Important failures are logged with useful diagnostic context.
* [ ] Logs do not contain sensitive information.
* [ ] Metrics or traces are added where the change affects a critical workflow.
* [ ] The team can determine whether the feature is working correctly after deployment.

### Documentation

* [ ] Relevant README, API or technical documentation is updated.
* [ ] Configuration or environment changes are documented.
* [ ] Deployment, migration or rollback steps are documented where required.
* [ ] Known limitations are recorded.

---

## Pull Request Evidence

The pull request should include:

* [ ] Link to this story.
* [ ] Summary of the change.
* [ ] Test evidence.
* [ ] Screenshots or recordings for UI changes.
* [ ] Security, accessibility or performance evidence where relevant.
* [ ] Deployment and rollback notes for higher-risk changes.
* [ ] Known risks or follow-up work.

---

## Definition of Done

The story is complete when:

* [ ] All acceptance criteria pass.
* [ ] Required tests pass locally and in CI.
* [ ] No critical or high-severity security or quality issues remain.
* [ ] The critical user or system journey has been validated.
* [ ] Documentation is updated.
* [ ] Code review is complete.
* [ ] The change has been deployed or is ready for deployment through the standard pipeline.
* [ ] Post-deployment validation is defined or completed.
* [ ] Any exception is documented with an owner and reason.

---

## Exceptions

None — all guardrails apply. The AdminConnect tenant list, detail and lifecycle-action screens are user-facing Next.js 16 surfaces, so the accessibility guardrail is in full effect, including keyboard-reachable suspension and offboarding dialogs with a required reason field that is programmatically associated with its control.

items.body:
As a team sharing a Lore installation, I want my data separated by enforced access rules and restorable on its own, so that another team can neither read it nor be restored over it.

<!-- lore-backlog-reconciled: 3971/full-review-v1 -->

## Backlog reconciliation

Reviewed against main at `3cb0d923c43d05e3ba03adb67b73c3acc61bce2d` using independent Codex review. Assessment: **partial**.

CNPG and backup infrastructure exist, but the pinned configuration still has one instance, 7d barman retention and a 30-day bucket lifecycle. Commented recovery bootstrap is not a restore runbook, executed drill or measured RTO/RPO, and does not establish tenant isolation.

### Remaining work

Document the deployment tenant boundary and decide per-tenant cluster versus RLS; implement/verify the chosen isolation, HA/retention alignment, recovery and per-team export runbooks, and an authorized timed restore drill.

### Evidence

- [infra/terraform/lore-db.tf:44–51](https://github.com/re-cinq/lore/blob/3cb0d923c43d05e3ba03adb67b73c3acc61bce2d/infra/terraform/lore-db.tf#L44-L51)
- [infra/terraform/lore-db.tf:88–96](https://github.com/re-cinq/lore/blob/3cb0d923c43d05e3ba03adb67b73c3acc61bce2d/infra/terraform/lore-db.tf#L88-L96)
- [infra/terraform/lore-db.tf:130–132](https://github.com/re-cinq/lore/blob/3cb0d923c43d05e3ba03adb67b73c3acc61bce2d/infra/terraform/lore-db.tf#L130-L132)
- [infra/terraform/lore-db.tf:152–167](https://github.com/re-cinq/lore/blob/3cb0d923c43d05e3ba03adb67b73c3acc61bce2d/infra/terraform/lore-db.tf#L152-L167)

Source review is not a claim of successful behavioral or production verification.

This assessment follows #3971 and PR #3972; it does not attribute all prior implementation to that change.

## Current acceptance criteria

- [ ] The tenant model and access isolation are explicit and enforced.
- [ ] CNPG has the agreed HA replica count and coherent recoverable retention.
- [ ] A timed restore and team export are demonstrated with measured RTO/RPO.

<details>
<summary>Original filing retained for scope, relationships, and audit history</summary>

### Schema-per-team is a retrieval partition, not tenant isolation (no RLS, one role); per-tenant recovery is whole-cluster PITR with no runbook or drill

asks about PostgreSQL-native RLS and restoring an individual tenant database. In code, a 'tenant' is a whole Lore deployment (one org). Team schemas only split the vector corpus, and one DB role reads all of them. Tasks, agent transcripts, memory and audit data share one schema per concern, with no RLS anywhere. Recovery: WAL archiving and daily base backups give cluster-level point-in-time recovery for 7 days on a single-instance cluster. There is no documented or tested restore procedure. Restoring one team or tenant means restoring the whole cluster to a side instance and dumping one schema.

**Evidence**
- `scripts/infra/setup-db.sh:97-144 (team schemas hold only <team>.chunks; all owned and read by the single `lore` role)`
- `apps/lore-api/src/transport/routes/context/search-context.ts:67-80 (team miss falls back to org_shared), chunk-schema-readers.ts:49 (browser unions every team schema)`
- `pipeline.*, memory.*, lore.* are org-wide schemas (setup-pipeline-schema.sh, setup-memory-schema.sh, setup-repos-schema.sh); grep finds no ROW LEVEL SECURITY / CREATE POLICY anywhere`
- `infra/terraform/lore-db.tf:131 (instances = 1), :177-183 (barman WAL archiver = PITR capable), :224-244 (daily base backup), :95 (7d retention) vs :44-51 (30d bucket lifecycle), :152-167 (restore only as a commented-out bootstrap block)`
- `runbooks/ holds only dark-factory-rollback.md and station-consolidation-cutover.md (no restore runbook)`

**Proposed change**
Before the call: write runbooks/db-restore.md (a CNPG recovery Cluster from the barman ObjectStore with a targetTime, then pg_dump -n <schema> for a partial restore). Run a timed restore drill and record the RTO and RPO. State the tenancy model honestly: deployment per tenant. Architecture options to bring: (a) a CNPG Cluster per tenant, which makes per-tenant PITR native and fits the existing terraform; (b) a shared DB with RLS on the memory, pipeline and lore tables keyed by repo or team, a per-request `SET app.tenant`, and non-owner app roles. Option (b) is a large migration across 32 models and needs an ADR. Also: move to instances >= 2 and align the 7d/30d retention.


Also: the CloudNativePG cluster runs `instances = 1` with 7-day backup retention against a 30-day bucket lifecycle (`infra/terraform/lore-db.tf`), and restore exists only as a commented-out `bootstrap.recovery` block. A per-tenant restore runbook and a rehearsal are missing.


_Found in a codebase audit on 2026-10-01 (main @ 0fabcf525); each point was checked against the code by a second reviewer._

</details>

milestone.title: M07 — Catalog & Media
milestone.description:
Objective: sellers publish products with verified images and stock; the catalog is queryable and tenant-safe.
Deliverables: product model v2; CRUD and lifecycle; public catalog query; taxonomy and seed; Mongo outbox + events; seller-status propagation; media authorization + verification; stock commands; seller portal product UI; security/perf suite.
Exit criteria: a seller publishes a product with a verified image and it appears via the public API; suspension hides products within 60 s; list p95 ≤ 400 ms on 10k products or deviations documented.
Depends on: M05, M06.

items.body:
<!-- planning-id: M07-12 -->

**Milestone:** M07 — Catalog & Media  
**Planning ID:** `M07-12`  
**Size:** S (planning estimate)  
**Requirements/traceability:** FR-SEL-05, FR-SEL-08

## Summary
Stores need a logo on their public profile.

## Dependencies
Blocked by:
- #69 — Media asset verification, metadata storage and cleanup
- #60 — Store profile settings

Do not start until the issues above are merged. If a dependency is missing, comment and stop.

## Current state
`sellers.logo_url` exists but cannot be set.

## Expected behavior
Logo uploader in `/settings` using signed upload → verify → `PATCH /sellers/me {logoAssetId}`; seller-service resolves the verified URL from media-service (internal lookup with a service token); same type/size rules; replacing a logo deletes the previous asset.

## Technical approach and files
Internal media lookup endpoint + seller update.

## Implementation steps
1. Internal lookup endpoint.
2. Seller update.
3. UI.
4. Tests.

## API / data / event / UI changes
`PATCH /sellers/me` accepts `logoAssetId`.

## Security, authorization and tenant isolation
The asset must belong to the same seller.

## Error handling, edge cases and recovery
Asset deleted meanwhile.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Given a verified asset of the seller, then the logo appears on the public store profile
- [ ] Given another seller's asset id, then 404.

## Testing requirements
Integration + Playwright.

## Documentation updates
READMEs.

_Update in-repository files listed here. Maintainer-held design documents live outside this repository; if you cannot see them, list the required changes in the pull request description._

## Definition of done
Standard DoD. (see "Reference: dod-standard" below for the standard checklist).

## Out of scope
Cropping tools.

## Embedded references
Essential constraints are inlined below so this issue is self-contained.

<details>
<summary>Reference: repo-context</summary>

**Repository:** pnpm 10 + Turborepo monorepo, Node 22, TypeScript. Apps (`apps/`): NestJS services `gateway` (4000), `auth-service` (4001), `product-service` (4002), `seller-service` (4003), `order-service` (4004), `payment-service` (4005), `notification-service` (4006), `media-service` (4007), `analytics-service` (4008); Next.js 15 apps `web` (3000), `seller-portal` (3001), `admin-portal` (3002). Shared packages (`packages/`): `contracts` (Zod schemas for DTOs/events), `auth-shared` (JWT/JWKS verification, guards), `kafka-client`, `logger` (Pino), `utils`, `ui`, `config` (eslint/tsconfig). Postgres (Drizzle) for auth/seller/order/payment; MongoDB (Mongoose) for product; Redis for rate limits/cache; Kafka-compatible broker for events. All datastores are managed cloud services — **no local Docker is required or may be introduced as a dependency**. Commands: `pnpm install`, `pnpm turbo run lint type-check test build --filter=<pkg>...`, `pnpm --filter <app> <script>`. Each service validates DTOs with Zod from `@betterbasket/contracts` (not class-validator) and exposes `GET /health`. Services compile to CommonJS.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Reference: frontend-conventions</summary>

Next.js 15 App Router, React 19, Tailwind 4, shadcn/ui, TanStack Query 5, Zustand 5, Better Auth React client, Zod schemas from `@betterbasket/contracts`. API access only through `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` (the gateway origin). JWT held in memory only (never `localStorage`), refreshed ≥60 s before expiry; route gating is client-side while APIs enforce authorization. All data views implement loading, empty, error-with-retry and stale/partial states and show the `requestId` from error envelopes. WCAG 2.2 AA (labels, focus, contrast, keyboard; axe has zero serious violations in CI). CSP (nonce-based), HSTS, `frame-ancestors 'none'` (seller/admin), `Referrer-Policy`, `Permissions-Policy`; third-party hosts allow-listed (Stripe, ImageKit); no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`; seller/admin portals `noindex`. No secrets in `NEXT_PUBLIC_*`. Money formatted from integer minor units with `Intl.NumberFormat`.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Reference: dod-standard</summary>

Implementation matches *Expected behavior*; every acceptance criterion passes with automated evidence; required tests added and green in CI (no skipped tests without a linked issue); lint, type-check, build, contract and migration checks pass; docs updated; security requirements satisfied including negative/authorization tests; no secrets, credentials or real customer/payment data in code, fixtures, logs or PR text; PR description complete; deployment verification performed when the issue affects a deployed environment.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Reference: agent-workflow</summary>

1. Read this whole issue; inspect the files named under *Technical approach*; confirm every item under *Current state* is still true (the codebase may have moved). 2. Verify each dependency issue is merged (see *Dependencies*); if a prerequisite is missing, stop and comment — do not re-implement it. 3. Post a short implementation plan as a comment before large changes. 4. Implement exactly the *Expected behavior*; respect *Out of scope*. 5. Write the tests listed under *Tests* (unit, integration, contract, E2E as applicable); run lint, type-check, tests and build for every touched package. 6. Review your own diff for security issues (authorization, tenant scoping, input validation, secret handling, logging of sensitive data) and regressions. 7. Update documentation named under *Docs* (in-repo files; if the maintainer's private design docs exist locally, update the affected sections too, otherwise list the required changes in the PR). 8. Check every acceptance criterion and quote the evidence (test names/output) in the PR description. 9. Open a reviewable PR: link this issue, list requirements covered, architectural impact, tests added, docs updated, migration/deployment impact. 10. If blocked or if a decision is unresolved, stop, comment with the question and options, and apply the `blocked:decision` label — do not guess or make architectural decisions that are not in this issue.

</details>

items.title: [Spec] P5 — Evidence, outcomes and business validation
items.body:
# P5 — Evidence, outcomes and business validation

Parent specification and coordination: https://github.com/JTBAZ/relay/issues/5

Status: ready for manager decomposition after assignment. No implementation, paid experiments or rollout dispatched by this issue.

## Problem Statement

Artists need useful recommendations but available metrics differ in definition, age and completeness. Without explicit evidence and workflow measurement, Relay could optimize vanity metrics or mistake feature activity for recurring value.

## Solution

Provide deterministic, provenance-bearing facts and outcomes to the manager, and measure whether the complete service saves artist effort and supports a viable recurring business.

## User Stories

1. As an artist, I want to see unavailable metrics distinguished from zero, so that missing data does not look like failure.
2. As an artist, I want to know whether a number is a captured total or period change, so that I can interpret it correctly.
3. As an artist, I want to see evidence tied to the right work and platform publication, so that unrelated performance does not influence my plan.
4. As an artist, I want to have commissions or memberships assessed separately from likes, so that my actual goal remains visible.
5. As an artist, I want to label outcomes I report myself, so that Relay does not imply independent verification.
6. As an artist, I want to see attribution uncertainty, so that estimates are not presented as proven conversions.
7. As an artist, I want to understand why a next-cycle change is suggested, so that I can accept or reject it intelligently.
8. As an operator, I want to measure completed releases and artist effort, so that we can distinguish useful management from queue activity.
9. As an operator, I want to measure repeat catalogue use and recurring sessions, so that we can test the archive's ongoing value.
10. As an operator, I want to measure model, storage, support and connector costs, so that subscription viability is assessed honestly.

## Implementation Decisions

- Own metric definitions, deterministic fact assembly, coverage/freshness, outcome semantics and workflow-value instrumentation. Reuse PiecePerformanceFacts, Goal Cycle fact packs, attribution/outcome snapshots and learning proposals.
- Preserve Work/Bundle, Relay Post and Platform Instance distinctions. Do not equate incompatible network metrics or relabel captured totals as period changes.
- Evidence records carry source, window/baseline, freshness, availability reason and attribution class. Latest unavailable observations must not silently resurrect older values as current evidence.
- Bind outcomes to plan/action/publication references; replayed receipts and observations cannot double-count success. Preparation completion is not publication completion.
- Supply facts for business goals where evidence exists; distinguish creator-reported, deterministic, estimated and unknown outcomes. Do not invent attribution when linkage is unavailable.
- Separate facts, generated interpretation and proposed experiments. P2/P3 own explanation behavior and grounding evaluation; P5 does not change measurements to fit a narrative.
- Design privacy-conscious telemetry for time/effort, corrections, repeat cycles, archive reuse, delivery failures and operating cost. Avoid raw private captions, patron identities or credentials in analytics metadata.
- Prepare a comparison/pilot protocol with baseline workflow and predeclared decision criteria. Running outreach, charging participants, changing prices or claiming validated demand is outside this specification.

## Testing Decisions

- Primary seam: authenticated evidence/outcome reads over real saved publication and plan records. Add focused deterministic metric tests where arithmetic and missingness require exact assertions.
- Cover stale/null data, unknown versus zero, baseline gaps, duplicate receipts, ambiguous links, changed source references and tenant isolation.
- Estimated conversions cannot satisfy a deterministic conversion target; likes do not substitute for sales.
- Prior art: PiecePerformanceFacts, Goal Cycle outcome/learning tests and attribution isolation integration. Feed the same evidence fixtures to P3 rather than parallel invented metric logic.

## Out of Scope

Exhaustive historical metrics, new scraping/trend providers, guaranteed growth, new attribution infrastructure without source evidence, billing changes, paid-pilot execution or external contact.

## Further Notes

Can inventory facts, publish definitions and build synthetic fixtures immediately. Integration needs P1 provenance, P2 plan/goal identity, P4 receipts and P6 correction/effort events. Exit: the manager can explain a completed or partial cycle from truthful facts, and the proposed pilot can distinguish usefulness, publication success and commercial outcomes.

The parent issue defines shared contract ownership, parallel waves, integration acceptance and shared-file serialization. Test boundaries were confirmed by the user: shared authenticated application operations, with focused connector and AI-quality evaluation seams. Preserve existing safety, approval and release requirements; reconcile older conflicting priorities with the current artist-manager direction.

Related pipelines: [P1](https://github.com/JTBAZ/relay/issues/6) · [P2](https://github.com/JTBAZ/relay/issues/7) · [P3](https://github.com/JTBAZ/relay/issues/8) · [P4](https://github.com/JTBAZ/relay/issues/9) · [P6](https://github.com/JTBAZ/relay/issues/11). Integration dependencies are described above; these links do not make all work wait for other pipelines to finish.
