items.title: Global admin panel: separate app, deployment, database, and admin user base
items.body:
## Summary

Create a standalone global admin panel — a separate application with its own deployment, its own database, and its own user base (admin accounts). It is not part of the main OSO app and is not accessible to regular OSO users.

## Motivation

Operational management of OSO instances (tenants/environments) requires a control plane that is isolated from the data it manages. A separate app and database ensures that admin access cannot be obtained through the regular OSO auth flow and that a compromise of one OSO instance does not grant admin access.

## Suggested scope

### Application
- Separate Next.js (or equivalent) application in the same monorepo or a dedicated repo
- Separate Docker Compose file and deployment pipeline
- Accessible at a distinct URL (e.g. `admin.ohmsweetohm.app` or an internal-only address)

### Authentication
- Completely separate user base from OSO — admin accounts are created and managed independently
- Strong authentication required (password + optional MFA); no SSO with OSO user accounts
- Admin sessions are scoped to the admin panel only

### Database
- Separate database storing only admin panel data: admin user accounts, tenant connections, audit log
- No shared tables or schemas with any OSO production database

## Blocks

- All other admin panel issues depend on this foundation

## Related

- Next issues in this initiative: tenant connection management, user/workspace management, registration control

items.title: Phase 3: OneDrive personal integration (Graph delta polling + save)
items.body:
# Phase 3 — OneDrive personal integration

Part of #3. Builds on Phase 2 (#5) — most of the plumbing (worker poller, retry harness, cloud settings page, schema changes) is shared.

**Effort:** ~4 days.

## Goals

- Mirror the Drive integration (Phase 2) for personal OneDrive using the existing Microsoft OAuth connection
- Recruiters using M365 without SharePoint can still use cloud inbox + save-to-cloud

## Architecture decisions

- **Scope: \`Files.ReadWrite.AppFolder\`** (safest) or \`Files.ReadWrite\` (broader, user-picked folder). Recommend \`Files.ReadWrite\` to match the Drive \`drive.file\` equivalent — app gets access to whatever the user points the folder picker at.
- **Polling via Graph delta**: \`GET /me/drive/root/delta\` with stored \`deltaLink\`. Similar cadence to Drive (30-60s).
- **Graph throttling is stricter** than Drive — honour \`Retry-After\` header rigorously. Retry harness from Phase 2 handles this.
- **Personal OneDrive only** — SharePoint site libraries are Phase 4 (#7).

## Implementation plan

### 1. OAuth scope extension
- Update \`src/app/api/auth/calendar/microsoft/route.ts\` — add \`Files.ReadWrite offline_access\` to scope string.
- Azure app registration — add API permission \`Files.ReadWrite\` (delegated). No admin consent required.

### 2. OneDrive API client
- \`src/lib/integrations/onedrive.ts\` — thin wrapper mirroring \`drive.ts\` shape:
  - \`listChangesSince(deltaLink)\`
  - \`downloadFile(itemId)\`
  - \`uploadFile(folderId, name, buffer)\` — \`PUT /me/drive/items/{folder-id}:/{filename}:/content\` for < 4MB; \`createUploadSession\` for larger
  - \`createFolder(parentId, name)\`
  - \`moveFile(itemId, targetFolderId)\`

### 3. Folder picker
- OneDrive doesn't have a Picker SDK as polished as Google's. Options:
  - Microsoft File Picker v8 (JavaScript SDK) — requires a \`messaging\` iframe host URL; more setup.
  - Hand-rolled tree browser using Graph \`/me/drive/root/children\` — simpler, ~0.5d work, acceptable UX.
- Recommend hand-rolled for v1.

### 4. Delta poller
- Extend \`src/worker/index.ts\` (or new \`src/worker/onedrive-poller.ts\`).
- For each tenant with OneDrive connection + \`inbox_folder_id\`:
  - Call \`GET /me/drive/items/{inbox_folder_id}/children/delta?token=<saved>\` (folder-scoped delta).
  - Filter by mime / extension.
  - Download via \`GET /me/drive/items/{id}/content\`.
  - Same candidate-insert + scoring pipeline as Phase 1 / Phase 2.
  - Move processed file into \`.processed\` child folder.
  - Save new \`@odata.deltaLink\` to \`sync_page_token\` (same column as Drive — each provider uses their own opaque token).

### 5. Save to OneDrive
- Mirror of Drive save: \`src/app/api/export/<category>/[id]/save-to-onedrive/route.ts\`.
- Return \`{ webUrl }\` for UI toast.

### 6. Auto-archive
- \`renderAndMaybeArchive\` helper already knows about Drive (Phase 2) — add OneDrive branch.

## Files to touch

- \`src/app/api/auth/calendar/microsoft/route.ts\` (scope update)
- Azure AD app registration (out-of-repo)
- \`src/lib/integrations/onedrive.ts\` (new)
- \`src/components/integrations/onedrive-folder-picker.tsx\` (new — hand-rolled tree)
- \`src/worker/onedrive-poller.ts\` (new, imported by worker entrypoint)
- \`src/app/api/export/<category>/[id]/save-to-onedrive/route.ts\` (new, 4 of them)
- \`src/lib/pdf/archive.ts\` (extend)
- \`src/app/(dashboard)/dashboard/settings/cloud-storage/page.tsx\` (extend to show OneDrive connection + picker)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Admin re-consents Microsoft OAuth and sees Files access added
- [ ] Admin picks a OneDrive folder as inbox; subsequent uploads are ingested within 60s
- [ ] Save-to-OneDrive button on each export works; returns webUrl
- [ ] Graph 429 throttling is handled without duplicate imports
- [ ] Auto-archive uploads every export to the configured folder when enabled

## Dependencies

- Phase 2 (#5) for shared schema, retry harness, worker structure, settings UI skeleton

## Non-goals

- SharePoint site libraries (#7)
- Graph change subscriptions (#8 — webhooks)
- Shared mailboxes or delegated admin scenarios

items.title: [ARCH-04] PostgreSQL Persistence, Tenant Isolation and Schema Evolution
items.body:
## Architecture implementation ticket

This architecture ticket is binding across the StrataAI2 functional PRDs.

### Adopted StrataAI2 override
Use PostgreSQL as the primary datastore, PostgreSQL RLS as defence in depth, **pgvector** for semantic retrieval, and ordered versioned migrations. PostgreSQL also hosts transactional outbox/job metadata initially. Do not add MongoDB, Elasticsearch, or a separate vector database without measured need and an ADR.

# ARCH-04 — PostgreSQL Persistence, Tenant Isolation and Schema Evolution

## 1. PRD identifier
ARCH-04

## 2. Feature name
PostgreSQL Persistence, Tenant Isolation and Schema Evolution

## 3. Executive summary
Use PostgreSQL through Npgsql with application tenant checks and PostgreSQL RLS as defence in depth, while adding disciplined versioned migrations for the larger product.

## 4. Problem statement
The expanded StrataAI functional suite requires a stable architecture contract. Without one, teams or coding agents could choose incompatible frameworks, data-access patterns, security boundaries, runtime modes, or release mechanisms.

## 5. Product objective
Provide durable multi-Organization persistence that cannot leak data across tenants and can evolve safely through CI and deployment.

## 6. User personas
- Software developer
- Technical architect
- DevOps/release engineer
- Security/privacy reviewer
- System administrator
- Quality engineer

## 7. User stories
- As a developer, I know exactly where this capability belongs and which interfaces it must use.
- As a release engineer, I can reproduce the same build locally and in CI.
- As a security reviewer, I can identify the trust and tenant boundaries.
- As an operator, I can run, diagnose, upgrade, and roll back the application.

## 8. Functional requirements
- **ARCH-04-FR-001** — Production SHALL use PostgreSQL 17+ through Npgsql.
- **ARCH-04-FR-002** — Every tenant-owned table SHALL carry a non-null `tenant_id`/Organization isolation key unless demonstrably global.
- **ARCH-04-FR-003** — Every tenant-owned production query SHALL require explicit tenant context.
- **ARCH-04-FR-004** — PostgreSQL RLS SHALL be enabled and forced on tenant-owned tables where technically applicable.
- **ARCH-04-FR-005** — Database access SHALL set transaction-local/application-local tenant context before RLS-protected operations.
- **ARCH-04-FR-006** — Missing/malformed/unauthorized tenant context SHALL fail closed.
- **ARCH-04-FR-007** — Schema evolution SHALL use ordered, versioned migrations; a single ever-growing bootstrap SQL string SHALL NOT be the long-term migration mechanism.
- **ARCH-04-FR-008** — Migrations SHALL be idempotent where appropriate and backward-safe for rollback/promotion strategies where feasible.
- **ARCH-04-FR-009** — Append-only audit storage SHALL reject ordinary UPDATE/DELETE.
- **ARCH-04-FR-010** — Core domain entities SHALL use normalized tables/constraints/indexes where correctness and queryability require it; JSONB MAY be used for flexible metadata/version snapshots.
- **ARCH-04-FR-011** — Production startup SHALL verify schema compatibility before accepting traffic.
- **ARCH-04-FR-012** — CI SHALL test migrations and RLS against a real ephemeral PostgreSQL instance.

## 9. Detailed interaction behaviour
All components must interact through the interfaces and trust boundaries defined by this PRD. Internal convenience must never bypass Organization isolation, authorization, audit, versioning, or provider boundaries.

## 10. Business / architecture rules
- Organization is the canonical tenant/domain boundary.
- `tenant_id` may be used as the infrastructure key representing an Organization.
- Production must fail closed rather than silently falling back to Demo behaviour.
- Build artifacts are immutable; environment-specific configuration is external.

## 11. Permission rules
Infrastructure must not broaden functional permissions. Authentication, Organization membership, Board permissions, governance roles, acting capacity, confidentiality, and owner-portal isolation remain server-authoritative.

## 12. Data requirements
Every tenant-owned persisted record must carry or be unambiguously scoped to an Organization/tenant. Schema constraints and indexes must enforce correctness where practical.

## 13. API requirements
APIs must use stable contracts, server-side authorization, consistent problem responses, idempotency where required, and explicit Organization context.

## 14. Real-time / event requirements
Events must preserve Organization context, correlation metadata, authorization-safe payloads, and stable event names. Event delivery must never expose data to an unauthorized subscriber.

## 15. UX requirements
Infrastructure states that affect users—Demo Mode, integration failure, stale version, degraded availability, pending AI processing—must have understandable and non-sensitive UI states.

## 16. Accessibility requirements
Architecture must preserve WCAG 2.2 AA capability. User-facing diagnostic or error states must be keyboard and screen-reader accessible.

## 17. Error and empty states
Fail closed on missing tenant/security configuration. Do not expose SQL, stack traces, secrets, provider credentials, or inaccessible-record existence.

## 18. Edge cases
Test missing configuration, dependency outage, container restart, partial deployment, stale client, duplicate/replayed integration messages, concurrent operations, failed migrations, and interrupted CI runs as applicable.

## 19. Non-functional requirements
Security, tenant isolation, deterministic builds, maintainability, observability, reproducibility, recoverability, and least privilege are mandatory.

## 20. Analytics / telemetry
Structured logs, metrics, traces, audit events, and build metadata must correlate failures and changes without recording secrets or prohibited personal data.

## 21. Dependencies
- ARCH-03
- ARCH-06
- ARCH-09
- ARCH-12
- PRD-20
- PRD-70

## 22. Out of scope
- Database-per-tenant as the default

## 23. Acceptance criteria
- **ARCH-04-AC-001** — GIVEN Organizations A and B WHEN A queries tenant-owned data THEN no B record can be returned even in tested paths with weakened application predicates.
- **ARCH-04-AC-002** — GIVEN a clean database WHEN all migrations run THEN the expected schema is produced deterministically.
- **ARCH-04-AC-003** — GIVEN an older supported schema WHEN the new image starts THEN forward migration succeeds or traffic is refused.
- **ARCH-04-AC-004** — GIVEN an audit row WHEN ordinary update/delete SQL executes THEN PostgreSQL rejects the mutation.

## 24. Test scenarios
Automated tests must cover all acceptance criteria plus material negative/security paths. CI must execute the tests relevant to this architecture boundary.

## 25. Definition of done
- All functional requirements are implemented or resolved by an approved ADR.
- Automated tests are green.
- CI validates the architecture boundary.
- Documentation matches the running system.
- No undocumented local-only dependency is required.

## 26. Open questions
- Select the migration tool/mechanism while retaining Npgsql-first persistence.


---

---

## Linked test cases
- [ ] **ARCH-04-TC-01** — Automated tests must cover all acceptance criteria plus material negative/security paths. CI must execute the tests relevant to this architecture boundary.

## Agent execution contract
- Treat this architecture ticket as a cross-cutting constraint for relevant PRD implementation tickets.
- Add automated tests for the acceptance criteria and reference ARCH/AC/test IDs.
- Do not silently substitute a different framework, datastore, message broker, deployment topology, authorization boundary, or CI release model.
- Link implementation PRs to this issue and include executed test evidence.

items.title: Proposal: add dr platform describe to report what an install supports
items.body:
**Update:** a prototype is up in #985, and this description now matches it. Changes since the first version: the report example below is corrected, the command ships ungated, and a schema test is added.

Field engineers who deploy Custom Applications to customer installs (self-managed and STS, often air-gapped) can't see what the install allows or requires until a call fails, usually after an upload. Which execution environment is valid for apps, which resource bundle, whether the caller holds a builder seat, whether apps deploy through the workload API: the answers differ per install, so a copied pipeline config breaks. Many of these engineers have little CI/CD experience. I'd like an agent with a skill to build a GitLab or GitHub pipeline for them from one structured answer.

Proposal: one read-only command, `dr platform describe`, that calls public routes only (`/version/`, public `/config`, `account/info`, `entitlements/evaluate`, `executionEnvironments`, `mlops/compute/bundles`) and prints a versioned JSON report with `--output-format json`, or a readable summary. A source that fails becomes `unavailable` with the reason and the other sections still return. The command exits 0 unless it can't reach the install or authenticate. There are no server changes, so it works on installs back to 11.12.

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "server": {"release": "11.14.0", "apiVersion": "2.49", "canonicalUrl": "https://dr.example.com"},
  "sections": {
    "install": {"status": "ok", "data": {"isEnterprise": true, "defaultAppResourceBundle": "cpu.xlarge"}},
    "seats": {"status": "ok", "data": {"seatLicenses": {"AGENTIC_PREDICTIVE_GOVERNANCE_BUILDER": true}}},
    "executionEnvironments": {"status": "ok", "data": {"items": [{"id": "5f1a...", "name": "[DataRobot] Python 3.12 Applications Base", "programmingLanguage": "python", "useCases": ["customApplication"], "hasSuccessfulVersion": true, "buildStatus": "success"}]}},
    "resourceBundles": {"status": "unavailable", "message": "HTTP 403: <body from the route>"}
  }
}
```

Two things the real installs showed. `seatLicenses` maps each license to whether the caller has it, and a license that is absent isn't enforced, so `{}` doesn't mean blocked. Environment names repeat on three of the four installs I looked at, so a reader has to pick by `id` and `hasSuccessfulVersion`. I ran the prototype against a multi-tenant, a single-tenant, and an air-gapped install behind a private CA (with `--ca-cert`).

Labs would own `cmd/platform/` and the JSON Schema (`docs/schemas/`), and the CLI maintainers would review. Not in scope: a server endpoint, an MCP tool, reachability checks.

Questions:

- Is a new top-level `platform` the right place, or would you rather extend `dr auth check`?
- Is it OK for Labs to own `cmd/platform/` and the schema? The PR adds CODEOWNERS lines for `@datarobot-oss/labs`.
- Should the report stay facts only (my preference, and what the PR does), or include verdicts like "you can create an app"?
- Tests check the report against the schema, which adds one test-only dependency, `santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema`. Is that fine?

Tech spec (internal): https://datarobot.atlassian.net/wiki/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=8154153229

items.title: security: replace unconditional runtime RLS policies with tenant/store isolation
items.body:
## Production blocker
Migration `db/migrations/0033_security_prodx_app_role.sql` grants DML on all public tables and creates a policy for every table with `USING (true) WITH CHECK (true)` for `prodx_app`. This makes RLS effectively non-restrictive for the runtime role and does not enforce organization/store boundaries. `0034_security_enable_rls_all_tables.sql` then enables RLS across the public tables.

This is confirmed by inspecting the migration and applying the current migration set to an isolated PostgreSQL 17 test instance. Do not apply migration 0033 to production as written.

## Required engineering work
- Inventory every public table and classify it as tenant/store scoped, global reference data, or internal migration/operations data.
- Trace authenticated principal organization/store context through HTTP routes, services, repositories, connection pool, and transaction boundaries.
- Design transaction-local, connection-safe tenant context for database RLS (no session state leaking between pooled requests; no client-supplied tenant identity).
- Add RLS policies with least privilege using the verified server-established context. Internal/global tables must receive explicit policies or privileges justified by schema-level evidence.
- Remove broad DML grants where not required; preserve required financial/inventory atomicity, idempotency, and audit behavior.
- Add PostgreSQL integration tests proving cross-store and cross-organization SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE are denied, allowed same-store operations work, and pooled connections cannot leak tenant context across requests.
- Verify migrations upgrade/downgrade and policy catalog; do not weaken or skip security gates.
- Update migration 0033 before deployment or add a deterministic follow-up migration that safely removes its broad policies; ensure fresh-install and upgrade paths converge without duplicate migration heads.

## Acceptance criteria
1. No `prodx_app` policy has unconditional `USING (true)` or `WITH CHECK (true)` on tenant-scoped data.
2. Runtime role remains `NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS`; it cannot read or mutate another tenant/store's rows even when application SQL omits a store predicate.
3. Tenant context is derived from authenticated server principal, set transaction-locally, and cleared automatically on commit/rollback/release.
4. PostgreSQL integration tests demonstrate isolation and pooled-connection reuse.
5. Full required CI, database/security/architecture gates pass.
6. No production migration/deploy until these conditions and live runtime verification pass.

## Related
- PR #265: https://github.com/Prodx-organization/PRODX-POS/pull/265
- Current production `/api/v1/healthz`: HTTP 200
- Current production `/api/v1/readyz`: HTTP 503 (request ID `3c0511b5-c9f8-42bf-9582-f1ab29714b43`)
- Current status remains **NOT PRODUCTION READY**.

The real image readiness fixture stopped at setup.py:38 with AttributeError before any readiness verdict. The same fixture passed on pinned 19 source 8b87b900.

This does not change Q870's decision or create a new migration stream. Include the typed config-parameter callers in the already scoped ports: disable_odoo_online#63 (expiration), shared-addons#83 (settings and other callers), devkit#278 (runtime/data/bootstrap adapters), and the respective tenant ports. If that read establishes approved work should stop, escalate through direction instead of closing it here.

items.title: Recruiter bot: parameterized quick-commands (command→tool routing, bypass Claude Code)
items.body:
Durable tracker for: рекрутёрский бот — параметризованные quick-команды (команда → тул, минуя Claude Code сессию).

Source doc (full checklist, repo map, test plan per step, 7 risks): https://instant-publish.trainedassist.store/p/recruiter-bot-checklist

## Order of work (each step closes its own test block from the doc before moving on)

- [x] **Step 1 — routing command→tool (§1.1)** — PR #622: new `/action` endpoint in `trained-assist-agent` that accepts `{tool, params}`, validates, calls `callTool()` from `src/mcp-skills/registry.js` directly — bypassing the Claude Code runner entirely. Same auth contour as `/run`. Tests: no session-store entry created; unknown tool → 400; missing required param → 400; missing auth → 401; latency vs current Claude-runner path (should be an order of magnitude faster).
- [ ] **Step 2 — unified param schema (§1.2)**: `commands-registry.json` gets `params: [{name, type, required}]` for new forward-to-tool commands + one shared parser (last param is greedy — takes rest of line). Do NOT rewrite existing local commands. Regression snapshot of current parser behavior before touching it.
- [ ] **Step 3 — 6-10 commands from the catalog (§1.3)**, starting with `/eval`, `/review`, `/send_message`. **BLOCKED until the confirm-flow architecture for `/send_message` and `/reject` is decided** (risk #5 below) — bare command must NOT actually send/reject, needs an explicit second step (`confirm` suffix or TTL'd pending-action). Test on a test vacancy, not live candidates. Also test `force` param for guard bypass, and command menu isolation between recruiter bot (`--env recruiter`) and main bot.
- [ ] **Step 4 — "command center" page (§1.5)**: one page (`/hh/commands` or extend `/hh/review`) listing available quick-commands + last result/artifact link per command. Not one page per tool. Playwright: HMAC-token auth works, all interactive elements have `data-testid`, mobile-width check.
- [x] **Step 5 — CLAUDE.md rule (§1.7)** — bundled into PR #622: document "recruiter-quick-action MCP tools must call OpenRouter, never open a Claude Code session" as a hard rule + cheap CI grep/lint step that fails if a new file under `src/mcp-skills/tools/*hh*` or `*recruiter*` imports the Claude Code runner.
- [ ] **Step 6 — replicate pattern** to other MCP domains (flexi, applylink, etc.) once HH proves out.

## Cross-cutting regression tests (before any merge, not optional)
- [ ] Free-text messages to both bots still go to the Claude runner as before (new short path must not swallow unrecognized commands)
- [ ] After deploy: verify via `wrangler deployments list` (or equivalent) that the NEW version is actually live — not just "PR merged, build silently failed" (happened before with `/persona` / duplicate `cmdStop`)
- [ ] After `commands-registry.json` changes: rebuild + redeploy `scripts/set-commands-recruiter.js`, otherwise Telegram autocomplete goes stale even if backend routing is correct

## Risks (already hit these in past iterations of this project — see full doc for detail)
1. "Merged" ≠ "live in prod" — verify against the real URL, not the PR state
2. Two repos, one feature (agent has the tool, gateway `trained-assist-tg-bot` must register the command or user sees "Неизвестная команда")
3. PR pipeline doesn't auto-merge (no GitHub Pro on private repos) — budget manual merge+deploy time
4. Recruiter bot Worker has its OWN secrets (`--env recruiter`) — new env vars must be added there too, separately from prod
5. Bypassing Claude Code loses the implicit safety pause it gave before send/reject — direct command→tool path needs an EXPLICIT two-step confirm designed before Step 3 starts (the one real architectural fork in this plan)
6. Cheap LLMs are not free/unlimited — reuse `hh-quick.js`'s existing 4-min cache pattern for `/action` rather than inventing new rate-limiting
7. `projects/` abstraction (PR #477) must be verified actually deployed before relying on it for artifact paths — don't trust memory of an earlier recon

## Repo map
- `trained-assist-agent` (this repo) — brains, HH tools (`src/mcp-skills/tools/90-hh.js`, `92-hh-proactive.js`), quick-command pattern (`src/hh-quick.js`), web routes (`src/server.js`)
- `trained-assist-tg-bot` — Telegram gateway (Cloudflare Worker), `commands-registry.json`, `src/handlers/commands.js`, recruiter bot = `[env.recruiter]` in `wrangler.toml`
- Recruiter bot `@super_recruiter_assistant_bot` already deployed and live (Worker `trained-assist-tg-bot-recruiter`)

Started 2026-09-15. Auto-continuation across sessions — check this issue's checkboxes for what's already done before redoing analysis.

items.title: Report card: tenant-wide photographer summary — gear, subjects, recurring faults, and curation behaviour
items.body:
## Motivation

#85 scopes a report card to a single shoot, gated at 100+ images, summarising
acceptance rate and defect frequency. Working the design against the live
catalogue, two things changed:

1. **The useful unit is the photographer, not the shoot.** A per-shoot card
   answers "how did this outing go". The question people actually ask is "what
   do I keep getting wrong, and is it me or my kit" — which only has an answer
   across everything they have uploaded. The aggregation is the same code with
   one fewer filter, so this supersedes #85's framing rather than competing
   with it.
2. **It needs its own page.** Not a panel in the gallery. It is read
   occasionally and deliberately, like the usage view, not while triaging.

This issue covers the tenant-wide version end to end. #85 stays open as the
narrower per-shoot variant, which becomes a filter on this once it exists.

## Proposed scope

A dedicated page, fed by one tenant-scoped endpoint, with seven sections:

| # | Section | Content |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Headline | Total images, keeper rate, trend over recent months |
| 2 | Your gear | Bodies and lenses by frame count, grouped by class (mirrorless / DSLR / mobile / compact), **each with its own keeper rate**; body×lens pairings where the sample supports it |
| 3 | What you shoot | Genre split (wildlife / landscape / nature / portrait / street / macro / architecture / event), focal-length bands, ISO bands, lighting |
| 4 | Recurring mistakes | Canonicalised fault families ranked by severity-weighted frequency, each showing how often it is severe and the reject-rate delta of frames carrying it |
| 5 | Known issues for your gear | Documented characteristics of the bodies/lenses in use — **only shown when this photographer's own images corroborate them** (see below) |
| 6 | How you curate | **Conditionally rendered.** Manual-decision behaviour: override rate, direction, and which faults this person forgives (see below) |
| 7 | Three things to change | Consolidation of 4, 5 and 6 into concrete technique/settings actions, each backed by the count it came from |

Section 2 is what makes this worth building: it is where someone learns that
their older body keeps a higher share than their newer one, or that one of two
telephotos underperforms the other at the same focal length. Nothing in the
product surfaces that today.

## Current state

Verified by reading live records, not by reading the schema.

| Capability | Status |
|---|---|
| Per-image defect detail stored | ✅ live — per image, no rollup anywhere |
| Composition analysis stored | ✅ live — present on ~99% of enriched records |
| EXIF camera string stored | ✅ live — present on ~99% of records |
| EXIF lens string stored | ✅ live — ~97%, of which a small share is unusable junk |
| Image embeddings stored | ✅ live — present on ~99% of enriched records |
| Tenant-scoped curation counts | ✅ live |
| Manual-override signal stored | ✅ live — but present on **~0.2% of images** (see section 6) |
| Defect-type rollup | ⬜ not implemented, and **blocked** — Blocker 1 |
| Genre rollup | ⬜ not implemented, and **blocked** — Blocker 2 |
| Gear rollup | ⬜ not implemented, and **blocked** — Blocker 3 |
| Gear-issue knowledge base | ⬜ does not exist |
| Report-card endpoint / page | ⬜ not implemented |

## Blockers found while planning

These are why this is not a straightforward aggregation. Each was found by
reading stored records; none is visible from the code.

### Blocker 1 — the stored defect vocabulary is not the defect taxonomy in code

The pipeline defines ~52 distortion types across 8 super-categories. The model
emits a different, smaller vocabulary, and nearly all of it is stored under
super-category `other` — so grouping by super-category produces one bucket
holding almost everything. Approximate share of images carrying each:

| Emitted type | ~% of images | In the defined taxonomy? |
|---|---|---|
| `exposure` | 71% | no |
| `sharpness` | 71% | no |
| `composition` | 62% | no |
| `noise` | 48% | no |
| `dynamic_range` | 42% | no |
| `low_light` | 40% | no |
| `white_balance` | 36% | no |
| `motion_blur` | 6% | yes |
| `chromatic_aberration` | 3% | yes |

Three distinct problems inside that:

- **Near-duplicate spellings fragment counts.** `sharpness` /
  `sharpness_on_subject` / `sharpness_on_the_subject`; `low_light` /
  `low_light_handling`; `focus` / `focus_accuracy`; `blur` / `motion_blur` /
  `severe_blur`.
- **Several entries are not faults.** `catch_light` (~12% of images),
  `subject_dominance` (~7%), `subject_anchored_composition`, `negative_space`,
  `depth_layers` and even `subject_label` are composition *observations* filed
  in the same list. Rolled up naively, the card would tell a wildlife
  photographer that catch-light is their third most common mistake.
- **~10% of all entries carry severity `none`** — records of a defect being
  *absent*. Counting them inverts the meaning of the section.

Fix: a canonicalisation layer keyed on what the model actually emits (sourced
from a census of stored values, not the prompt enum), folding spellings into
~12 fault families, classifying each family as fault vs observation, and
dropping severity `none`. Ships with a test that fails when an unmapped type
becomes common, so future prompt revisions surface instead of silently landing
in `other`.

This is a defect in its own right — it also means any current or future
grouping by defect super-category is meaningless. Happy to split it out.

### Blocker 2 — genre is populated on a small fraction of the catalogue

Related to #72. The categorical tags do now populate on newly processed images,
but the back catalogue predates that rollout, so the stored genre signal covers
only a few percent of all images. Share of each month's images carrying a genre:

- Two months ago: effectively zero
- Last month: ~19%
- This month: ~65%

Same shape for lighting, subject clarity and mood. Note that even the current
month is not at 100%, which is worth understanding separately under #72.

Fix, and the reason this is tractable: the image embedding is already stored on
~99% of enriched records. Genre can be recovered by encoding a small set of
label prompts with the text encoder that already exists for semantic search and
cosine-ranking stored embeddings against them — a CPU matrix multiply, no GPU
time, no reprocessing, no re-reading originals. Genre becomes a derived field
carrying a confidence value, and improves on its own as natively tagged images
accumulate.

Dependency: the semantic-search read path is currently flag-disabled. The
embeddings are written regardless; only the read-side encoder is gated.

### Blocker 3 — gear strings are raw EXIF and nothing normalises them

No component parses camera or lens strings; they are passed through verbatim.
Consequences visible in stored data: case variants split one manufacturer into
separate makes; genuinely different lens revisions sit adjacent with no
indication they are related; and a meaningful number of records carry EXIF junk
in the lens field (zero-value focal/aperture strings, unknown-aperture
placeholders) that must never reach a reader.

Fix: a normaliser producing a stable key, display name, brand and **class**
(mirrorless / DSLR / mobile / compact / medium-format / unknown) per body and
lens. Class is what supports the DSLR-vs-mobile breakdown. Junk lens values
collapse to "not recorded" rather than being rendered.

## Section 6 — curation behaviour, and why it must be conditional

The card should also reflect **how the person curates**, not only what the
pipeline concluded: how often they override a verdict, in which direction, and
which faults they systematically forgive or punish. Proposed content:

- Override rate — share of decided images where the person disagreed with the
  automated verdict.
- Direction — rescued rejects vs demoted accepts. These mean very different
  things: consistently rescuing rejects suggests the rule engine is too strict
  for this person's subject matter (compare #58), while demoting accepts
  suggests a higher personal bar than the engine's.
- Forgiveness profile — fault families this person keeps frames despite, and
  families they reject on even when the engine accepted.
- Review follow-through — how much of the review queue actually gets resolved
  versus left sitting.

This is also the visible half of a path the product already anticipates: the
per-user analysis prompt is seeded from the global one and intended to learn
from manual overrides. Surfacing the override signal is a sensible precursor to
acting on it.

**But it must be conditionally rendered, and today it would almost never
render.** Measured across the live catalogue, roughly **0.2% of images carry any
manual curation decision at all** — the overwhelming majority of verdicts are
never touched by a human. So:

- The section appears only when an account has enough manual decisions to say
  anything (proposed floor: 50 decided images, tuned once real usage exists).
- Below that it is absent entirely — not an empty state, not a zero, not a
  placeholder. A "0% override rate" reads as a finding about the photographer
  when it is really a finding about feature adoption.
- Every figure in it is stated against its denominator ("across 63 decisions
  you made"), never as a bare percentage.

That low number is itself worth noting as a product signal: either people are
content with the automated verdicts, or manual curation is not discoverable
enough to be used. The report card will not answer which — but it should not
pretend to either.

## Gear knowledge base — design constraint

Section 5 is the highest-value part and the easiest to get wrong. A model asked
to free-associate about a camera body will produce fluent, plausible,
unfalsifiable claims. The rule adopted here:

> A documented gear characteristic is only shown when the photographer's own
> images corroborate it.

Each entry states the claim **and** the measurable signature required before it
surfaces. Examples of that shape:

- A dense APS-C body's high-ISO noise entry fires only if that body's noise and
  low-light fault rate above ISO 1600 materially exceeds its own rate below
  ISO 800.
- A telephoto zoom's slow-long-end entry fires only if frames at the long end
  show a higher exposure/low-light fault rate than the same body's shorter-focal
  frames.
- A heavy prime's shake entry fires only if motion blur concentrates in that
  lens's frames at slow shutter speeds.

That turns the section from trivia into a diagnosis and makes every entry
falsifiable against the catalogue. The knowledge base is hand-curated and
version-controlled — never model-generated prose. Where a body has no entry,
the section says so.

## Architecture

- One tenant-scoped endpoint; tenant identity from the token, never the request.
  Optional time window and cache-bypass parameters.
- **Always served from a pre-warmed snapshot, never computed inline.** Image
  records are large because they carry the embedding; a high-volume account's
  catalogue is well beyond what can be read within the existing request timeout
  ceiling at current task sizing. The card is built by a background warm pass on
  the 500/200 trigger above, lock-guarded, each account in its own try block so
  one failure cannot leave the rest cold. The snapshot needs no TTL — it is valid
  until enough new images exist to change it.
- The aggregation query uses a narrow projection that **excludes the embedding**,
  cutting transferred bytes by roughly an order of magnitude. Worth recording
  that a projection reduces transfer and deserialisation time but *not* read
  capacity — the store charges on full item size regardless. This is a latency
  fix, not a cost one, and latency is what decides whether the feature works.
- Reads via the recency index so date windowing is a key condition rather than a
  filter over the whole partition. The existing curation-stats path is untouched.
- Sections degrade independently — a thin signal yields an honest "not enough
  data yet" state, never a 500 and never an empty chart.

## Cadence and threshold

**First card at 500 images; rebuild every 200 new images after that.** Decided —
see the follow-up comment for the full rationale and the trigger design.

Below 500 a photographer usually has one body, one lens and one outing, so every
comparative row is a sample of one and the gear section has nothing to say.
Tying updates to 200 new images means the numbers only move when the underlying
behaviour could have moved.

The trigger reads the cumulative image counter already on each account's config
record — one small key lookup per account, no scan — and rebuilds when
`total >= 500` and `total - built_at_count >= 200`. A 30-day staleness ceiling
stops a card freezing for someone who uploads 199 images and stops; manual
refresh stays available, rate-limited.

Every derived figure still states its coverage ("based on N of M images
classified") until the genre backfill lands. Section 6 has its own, separate
floor as described above.

Consequence to accept: at 500, three of roughly fourteen accounts qualify today.
Account sizes fall into two clean groups — three above 1,000 images, everything
else at 240 or fewer — so the below-threshold state is what most people will see,
and it should show progress toward 500 rather than read as an empty card.

## Phases

1. **Data truth** — defect canonicaliser, fault-vs-observation split, severity
   filtering, gear normaliser with class assignment, junk-EXIF handling. Pure
   functions, unit tested, plus the drift test. No endpoint yet.
2. **Aggregation + endpoint** — service, section response schema, snapshot key,
   warm stage.
3. **The page** — new route and nav entry, built on existing dashboard patterns.
   No new frontend dependencies.
4. **Gear knowledge base** — curated entries for the bodies and lenses actually
   in use, each with its corroborating signature, plus the evidence gate.
   Section stays flag-hidden until entries are reviewed.
5. **Genre recovery** — zero-shot classification over stored embeddings.
   Separable; everything above ships without it, showing honest coverage
   figures until it lands.

Section 6 rides along with phase 2 — it is cheap, since the override signal is
already stored — but will stay invisible in practice until manual curation sees
real use.

Roughly 2.5–3 weeks of single-developer work. No new infrastructure: it reuses
the existing always-on service, the existing snapshot cache, and embeddings
already being written.

## Open questions

- Does #85 close in favour of this, or stay open as the per-shoot filter?
- Should Blocker 1 be split into its own defect issue, given it affects any
  grouping by defect super-category and not just this feature?
- Genre recovery in the first release, or ship with honest low coverage and add
  it after?
- Is a ~0.2% manual-decision rate expected, or does it point at a discoverability
  problem worth its own issue?

## Non-goals (v1)

- Cross-tenant or admin-facing reporting.
- Notifications when a report card updates.
- Any change to how images are analysed — this reads only what is already
  stored.

Related: #85 (per-shoot original), #72 (categorical tag coverage), #93 (the
critique/improvements split whose phrasing discipline section 7 follows), #58
(technique-detection bias against wildlife subjects, which interacts with
sections 2 and 6).

items.body:
## Objective

Replace the inline-style `/dashboard` shell with the PaintPro S37 operational hierarchy using the repository's existing shadcn/Tailwind primitives and live Convex data.

Source target: `PaintPro_Source_Kit/manifest/primary-screen-map.csv` → S37, backed by `originals/paintpro_os_unified_operations_dashboard__screen.png`.

## Permitted files

- `apps/web/src/app/dashboard/page.tsx`
- New dashboard-local components, helpers, route error/loading states, and tests under `apps/web/src/app/dashboard/`

## Exclusions

- No edits to pipeline, shared header/proxy/auth, global styles/tokens, shared UI primitives, Convex schema/functions, manifests, or other product lanes.
- No static sample business data, invented revenue, or fake charts.
- Preserve the current `api.backend.listLeads` / `listJobs` query boundaries and tenant membership enforcement.

## Acceptance

- [ ] S37 hierarchy is recognizable: operational header, live metric cards, recent records, and quick actions.
- [ ] Metrics and records are derived only from live Convex results and are labeled honestly when bounded to the loaded page.
- [ ] Existing lead/job/invoice creation mutations remain reachable.
- [ ] Loading, empty, unauthenticated, and query/route error states are actionable.
- [ ] Phone layout remains usable without fixed desktop widths.
- [ ] shadcn primitives and semantic Tailwind tokens are used; no inline styles or raw color values.
- [ ] Dashboard-local tests cover derived metrics, record ordering, and labels.

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Situation

The HMS platform is greenfield. Today there is no telemetry pipeline at all: Go services emit unstructured `log.Printf` output to stdout, there are no metrics beyond whatever Knative and Istio expose by default, and there is no request correlation across the modular monolith, NATS JetStream consumers, Temporal workers and the Next.js consoles. When a request fails there is no way to answer the only three questions that matter — which tenant, which workflow, and where in the chain it broke.

This is not merely a convenience gap. Concretely:

- **EmergencyConnect is life-critical.** An ambulance dispatch that stalls between `AmbulanceDispatched` being published and the crew's device receiving it is a patient-safety event. Without distributed traces spanning HTTP → JetStream → device push, the on-call SRE has no evidence of where the latency sits and no basis for the capacity headroom the brief mandates for this product.
- **Noisy-neighbour degradation is invisible.** The platform is shared-schema multi-tenant with row-level security. Per-tenant rate limits and quotas are meaningless if we cannot attribute latency, error rate and database time to a tenant.
- **CERT-In imposes log-retention obligations** and rapid incident-reporting windows on entities operating in India. Retention cannot be evidenced against ad-hoc container stdout that Kubernetes rotates away.
- **PHI leakage through telemetry is a DPDP Act 2023 exposure.** Naïve instrumentation captures full URL paths, request bodies and SQL parameters. `GET /patients/abha/91-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX` in a span name, or a patient name in a GORM query log, is unlawful processing routed to a third-party backend, and it is the DPO who carries that.

Affected: SRE on-call, every backend engineer debugging a cross-module failure, the hospital admin who wants an SLA dashboard, and the DPO who must attest to what leaves the country boundary.

Instrumenting this after fifteen products exist is an order of magnitude more expensive than establishing the shared library now. This issue is a hard dependency for SLA dashboards, tenant-level monitoring and clinical workflow monitoring.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** platform SRE and backend engineer
**I want** every HMS service, worker and console to emit correlated OpenTelemetry traces, metrics and structured logs with tenant and workflow attribution and no PHI
**So that** I can diagnose a failure across HTTP, events, workflows and the database within minutes, attribute load to a tenant, and evidence retention without breaching DPDP.

### Scope

**In scope**

* A shared Go module (`pkg/telemetry`) providing a single `Init(ctx, ServiceConfig)` that wires the OTLP trace, metric and log exporters, resource attributes (`service.name`, `service.version`, `deployment.environment`, `country.profile`), and a coordinated shutdown.
* Automatic instrumentation: `otelgin` middleware, `otelgorm` callbacks for PostgreSQL 16, Redis client hooks, and outbound `http.Client` propagation.
* **Trace context propagation across NATS JetStream** — W3C `traceparent`/`tracestate` injected into message headers on publish and extracted on consume, so an event chain is one trace.
* **Temporal propagation** via a custom `ContextPropagator` so workflow and activity spans join the originating request trace.
* Tenant attribution: `tenant.id` and `facility.id` promoted from the tenant-scoped data-access layer onto every span, metric exemplar and log record.
* A PHI redaction layer: allowlist-based span attributes, parameterised route templates as span names (`GET /patients/:id`, never the resolved value), GORM query text without bound parameters, and a `zap`/`slog` handler that drops known-sensitive keys.
* RED metrics (rate, errors, duration) per route and per JetStream subject, plus JetStream consumer lag and Temporal task-queue backlog gauges.
* Browser telemetry from the Next.js 16 consoles: page load and route-change spans propagating `traceparent` into API calls.
* Collector deployment as an ArgoCD-managed DaemonSet with tail sampling, per-country export routing, and a documented retention configuration.

**Out of scope**

* **SLA dashboards and tenant-level monitoring UI** — consumes this pipeline; owned by the sibling Observability issue for SLA dashboards.
* **Synthetic monitoring and error tracking (Sentry-class) product analytics** — separate cards under the Observability epic.
* **Alerting rules, escalation policy and on-call rotation** — defined once golden signals exist; separate SRE issue.
* **Audit logging.** Tamper-evident audit records for record access, prescriptions and break-glass are a clinical-compliance concern with different retention and immutability guarantees, owned by the Audit epic. Telemetry is diagnostic and explicitly must not be the audit trail.
* **Load testing and capacity planning** — depends on this issue but is owned by the SRE reliability epic.

---

## Recommended Solution

### Shared library

One Go module consumed by every service, so instrumentation is opt-out rather than opt-in.

```go
// pkg/telemetry
type Config struct {
    ServiceName    string
    Version        string
    Environment    string // dev | staging | prod
    CountryProfile string // IN (NP, AF later)
    OTLPEndpoint   string // in-cluster collector, never a public endpoint
    SampleRatio    float64
}

func Init(ctx context.Context, c Config) (shutdown func(context.Context) error, err error)
```

`Init` installs a `TracerProvider` with a parent-based sampler, a `MeterProvider` with an OTLP push exporter on a 15s interval, and an `slog` handler bridging logs to OTLP while retaining stdout JSON for local development. Services call it once in `main` and `defer shutdown`.

### Tenant attribution

The tenant-scoped data-access layer is already the single choke point through which no query may pass without its tenant (architectural rule 1). Extend the same `TenantContext` to carry a `baggage` entry, and register a `SpanProcessor` that copies `tenant.id`/`facility.id` onto every span at start. This means attribution is structurally guaranteed rather than dependent on each developer remembering — the same argument that justifies the RLS choke point.

### PHI redaction

Two defences, because one is not enough for regulated data:

1. **In-process** — a `SpanProcessor` that filters attributes against an allowlist. Anything not on the list is dropped, not redacted, so a new field cannot leak by default. Route templates come from Gin's `c.FullPath()`, never `c.Request.URL.Path`. GORM's callback logs `db.Statement.SQL.String()` only, never `db.Statement.Vars`.
2. **In the collector** — a `redaction` processor plus `attributes` processor as a backstop, blocking patterns for ABHA numbers, Aadhaar-shaped digit sequences, phone numbers and email addresses. A CI test asserts a known-PHI payload never reaches the exporter.

### NATS JetStream propagation

Domain events (`AppointmentBooked`, `PrescriptionIssued`, `LabResultReady`, `AmbulanceDispatched`, `ConsentGranted`/`ConsentRevoked`) are the primary inter-module path, so an untraced broker breaks every interesting trace.

```go
// publish
prop.Inject(ctx, natsHeaderCarrier(msg.Header))
// consume
ctx = prop.Extract(ctx, natsHeaderCarrier(msg.Header))
ctx, span := tracer.Start(ctx, subject+" process", trace.WithSpanKind(trace.SpanKindConsumer))
```

Publish and consume spans are linked by producer/consumer kind so the JetStream hop shows as real latency, and consumer lag is exported per durable as `messaging.jetstream.consumer.lag`.

### Metric surface

| Metric | Type | Key attributes |
|---|---|---|
| `http.server.request.duration` | histogram | `http.route`, `http.response.status_code`, `tenant.id` |
| `messaging.process.duration` | histogram | `messaging.destination.name`, `tenant.id` |
| `messaging.jetstream.consumer.lag` | gauge | `consumer`, `stream` |
| `db.client.operation.duration` | histogram | `db.operation.name`, `db.collection.name` |
| `temporal.workflow.task.backlog` | gauge | `task_queue` |

`tenant.id` is deliberately absent from high-cardinality DB metrics; tenant attribution there is carried on exemplars linking to traces instead, to keep the time-series count bounded.

### Collector and residency

Collector as a DaemonSet, ArgoCD-managed under `charts/apps/hms-otel-collector`. Data residency is a hard boundary (architectural rule 3), so the collector's export routing is per-country: the India deployment exports only to India-resident backends. Tail sampling keeps 100% of errors and of all EmergencyConnect traffic, and 5% of the remainder, so life-critical dispatch is never sampled away. Retention configured and documented to satisfy CERT-In log-retention obligations.

### Sequencing

Depends on the tenant-scoped data-access layer and the NATS JetStream event bus existing. Should land before the first product module ships so no service is written uninstrumented. The Collector Helm chart lands ahead of the library so services have somewhere to export.

### Risks

- **Cardinality explosion** from `tenant.id` on every series. Mitigated by bounding tenant attribution to the RED metrics above and using exemplars elsewhere; a collector-side cardinality limiter caps series per metric.
- **Telemetry becoming a hot path failure.** The OTLP exporter is non-blocking with a bounded queue that drops on overflow. A collector outage must degrade telemetry, never patient care — asserted by a test that black-holes the endpoint and confirms request latency is unaffected.
- **Redaction drift.** The allowlist is enforced by a CI test that fails when a span attribute is added without a corresponding allowlist entry.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** a patient books an appointment through MediConnect, which publishes `AppointmentBooked` to JetStream, consumed by a MediCore handler that starts a Temporal workflow and writes to PostgreSQL
**When** an engineer searches the trace backend by the response's `trace_id`
**Then** a single trace is returned containing the browser span, the Gin server span named `POST /appointments`, the JetStream producer and consumer spans, the Temporal workflow and activity spans and the GORM query spans, every span carrying `tenant.id`, `service.name` and `country.profile`, and no span attribute or log record containing a patient name, phone number, ABHA number or Aadhaar-shaped value.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** the OpenTelemetry Collector is unavailable (pods evicted, endpoint refusing connections)
**When** EmergencyConnect handles an ambulance dispatch request under normal load
**Then** the request succeeds within its usual latency budget, the exporter queue drops spans without blocking, a single rate-limited `telemetry export failed` log is emitted at warn level, the process does not panic or leak goroutines, and the `otel.exporter.dropped_spans` counter increments so the loss is itself observable.

### Edge Cases

* A JetStream message is redelivered after a consumer NACK — the retry produces a new span linked to the original rather than a duplicate trace, and redelivery count is recorded as an attribute.
* A Temporal workflow spans days and outlives its originating HTTP trace — workflow spans use span links to the initiating trace rather than an unbounded open parent span.
* A tenant on the schema-per-tenant premium tier — telemetry attribution works identically without leaking the tenant's schema name into span attributes.
* A request arrives from an untrusted external client carrying a forged `traceparent` header — the header is accepted for correlation but the sampling decision is not inherited from it, so an attacker cannot force 100% sampling and drive a cost or cardinality attack.
* Contractor-scoped access via FacilityConnect — a contractor's work-order request produces spans whose attributes contain no patient or clinical identifiers, consistent with their scoped-access boundary.
* Non-production environments — PHI never appears in non-prod (synthetic data only), and the redaction test suite runs against the same allowlist in every environment so a prod-only rule cannot be introduced.

---

## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team's agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
* [ ] Existing tests pass.
* [ ] No new flaky or skipped tests are introduced without justification.

### Security and Access

* [ ] Authentication and authorisation are enforced at the appropriate layer.
* [ ] Users and services can access only the data and actions they require.
* [ ] Input is validated and sensitive information is not exposed in logs or errors.
* [ ] Secrets and credentials are not stored in source code.
* [ ] Security and dependency scans pass.
* [ ] Tenant, account or customer isolation is tested where applicable.

### Accessibility and User Journey

* [ ] The primary user journey works from start to completion.
* [ ] Loading, empty, success and error states are handled.
* [ ] Keyboard navigation and focus behaviour work correctly.
* [ ] Controls have clear labels and accessible names.
* [ ] The change meets the team's agreed WCAG accessibility level.
* [ ] The experience works across supported devices and browsers.

### Performance and Reliability

* [ ] The change does not introduce unnecessary API calls, database queries or processing.

## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** Any request, event or workflow across the platform is traceable end to end from a single `trace_id`, attributed to a tenant, with structured logs and RED metrics available for every route and JetStream subject.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** On-call can localise a failure to a service and dependency without adding instrumentation during the incident; tenant-level load attribution becomes possible, unblocking per-tenant quotas, SLA dashboards and capacity planning; CERT-In log-retention obligations are evidenced by configuration rather than assertion.
* **Success metric or validation method:**
  - 100% of Go services, JetStream consumers and Temporal workers report traces and RED metrics — verified by a conformance test asserting every deployed `service.name` appears in the metric store within 5 minutes of rollout.
  - Trace continuity ≥ 99% across the HTTP → JetStream → Temporal boundary, measured as the proportion of consumer spans with a valid remote parent over a 24-hour window.
  - Instrumentation overhead adds no more than **3 ms to p95** and **2% to allocated memory** on the EmergencyConnect dispatch endpoint, measured by load test with instrumentation on versus off.
  - **Zero** PHI-pattern matches in a 7-day sample of exported spans and logs, scanned by an automated job against the ABHA, Aadhaar, phone and email patterns.
  - Mean time to localise a fault (service + dependency identified) under 10 minutes in a deliberate game-day fault injection.
* **Monitoring period:** 30 days after the collector reaches production, with a cardinality and export-cost review at day 14.

items.body:
## Situation

The platform has no backup strategy beyond whatever CloudNativePG produces by default: a cluster-wide base backup plus WAL archive covering every tenant in the shared-schema database as one indivisible blob. That is adequate for total cluster loss and useless for everything hospitals actually ask for.

Three concrete failure modes are unaddressed. A single hospital corrupts its own data — a bad bulk import of a drug master, a mis-run ward merge, a ransomware event on a tenant's own workstation feeding bad edits through the API — and asks to be restored to 09:00 this morning. With a cluster-wide backup, restoring that tenant means restoring every tenant, discarding a day of clinical activity across dozens of hospitals. Second, a tenant offboards and contractually requires a complete, portable export plus proof that residual copies are destroyed; a cluster-wide backup guarantees their PHI persists in snapshots belonging to everyone else. Third, restore has never been tested — an untested backup is a hypothesis, not a control, and NABH accreditation surveyors, tenant DPOs and CERT-In post-incident reviews all ask for evidence of tested recovery, not a policy document.

Affected roles: the hospital admin who owns the recovery-point conversation with their board, the DPO who must evidence deletion under DPDP Act 2023 including from backups, the platform SRE running the restore at 02:00, and every clinical user whose records are the subject of the RPO/RTO commitment. Data residency compounds it: a backup written to a region outside India is a residency breach, not merely a policy lapse.

This is greenfield. Backup topology must be decided before tenant volume makes retrofit expensive, and it must build directly on the tenant-scoped storage paths (#29) and per-tenant keys (#30) already in this epic.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** platform SRE responsible for tenant recovery commitments
**I want** per-tenant logical backups and per-tenant object-store snapshots, each encrypted under that tenant's own key, written only within the tenant's country region, with automated restore verification
**So that** one tenant can be restored to a point in time without touching any other tenant, and every backup we hold is provably restorable and provably destroyable.

### Scope

**In scope**

* A per-tenant logical backup job producing a consistent, tenant-filtered dump of all RLS-scoped tables, plus per-tenant manifests of object-store keys under the tenant's prefix.
* Encryption of every backup artefact under the tenant's TEK from issue #30 — a backup must be unreadable if that tenant's key is shredded.
* Backup artefacts written only to a bucket in the tenant's country region, with the same `{country}/{tenant_id}/…` prefix discipline as #29 and IAM conditions preventing cross-region writes.
* Retention and RPO/RTO tiers driven by the tenant's subscription tier (standard: 24h RPO / 8h RTO; enterprise: 15min RPO via continuous WAL plus tenant-filtered PITR / 2h RTO), configured, not hard-coded.
* An orchestrated per-tenant restore into an isolated scratch database, with a dry-run mode that restores and validates without promoting.
* Automated weekly restore verification for a rotating sample of tenants, producing a signed verification record.
* Backup catalogue with size, row counts per domain, checksum, key version and residency region.
* Offboarding path: final export handed to the tenant, then backup destruction with an attestation.

**Out of scope**

* Cluster-level disaster recovery and cross-AZ failover of the CloudNativePG cluster — owned by the Infrastructure epic; this issue is about tenant-granular recovery, not cluster survival.
* Per-tenant encryption key material and crypto-shredding mechanics — issue #30 (this issue consumes the TEK and the shred attestation).
* The object path layout — issue #29.
* Analytics/OLAP warehouse backups — that store holds only de-identified aggregates and has its own lifecycle.
* Tenant self-service restore from the AdminConnect console — a later story; this issue delivers the operator-run capability and the API it will call.

---

## Recommended Solution

Orchestrate with Temporal — a tenant backup spans a database dump, an object manifest, encryption, upload, catalogue write and verification, and must be resumable and idempotent rather than a cron script that silently half-fails.

`TenantBackupWorkflow(tenant_id, tier)` runs on a schedule derived from the tier and executes activities:

1. `SnapshotConsistencyPoint` — open a repeatable-read transaction, record `pg_current_wal_lsn()` as the consistency point.
2. `DumpTenantTables` — stream each RLS-scoped table filtered by `tenant_id` through a Go writer with `SET app.tenant_id` applied, so the dump inherits the same isolation guarantee as the application. Reference tables owned by the platform (issue #34's global reference data) are recorded by version reference, not copied.
3. `SnapshotObjectManifest` — list the tenant's storage prefix and record `(storage_key, sha256, size, version)`; objects are already immutable, so the manifest plus retention lock is the snapshot.
4. `EncryptAndUpload` — AES-256-GCM with a fresh DEK wrapped under the tenant's current TEK version; upload to `backups/{country}/{tenant_id}/{backup_id}/`.
5. `WriteCatalogue` + publish `TenantBackupCompleted`.

`TenantRestoreWorkflow(tenant_id, backup_id, target, mode)` restores into a scratch CloudNativePG database, runs validation (row counts per domain against the manifest, referential integrity, RLS policy presence, a sample of decrypt round-trips), and in `dry_run` mode stops there and emits a verification record. In `promote` mode it requires a second approver and a stated incident reference before any write reaches the live cluster.

```sql
CREATE TABLE tenant_backup (
  backup_id       UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id       UUID NOT NULL,
  country_code    CHAR(2) NOT NULL,
  tier            TEXT NOT NULL,
  kind            TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (kind IN ('full','incremental','wal_segment')),
  consistency_lsn PG_LSN NOT NULL,
  storage_prefix  TEXT NOT NULL,
  key_version     INT NOT NULL,
  size_bytes      BIGINT NOT NULL,
  row_counts      JSONB NOT NULL,        -- {"encounter": 12043, "work_order": 88, ...}
  checksum        BYTEA NOT NULL,
  started_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  completed_at    TIMESTAMPTZ,
  state           TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (state IN ('running','completed','failed','verified','destroyed')),
  expires_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  legal_hold      BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, consistency_lsn, kind)
);

CREATE TABLE backup_verification (
  id          UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  backup_id   UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES tenant_backup(backup_id),
  verified_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  rto_seconds INT NOT NULL,
  findings    JSONB NOT NULL,
  passed      BOOLEAN NOT NULL
);
```

API surface (platform-operator scoped, AdminConnect):

* `GET  /api/v1/admin/tenants/{tenant_id}/backups`
* `POST /api/v1/admin/tenants/{tenant_id}/backups` — on-demand backup (e.g. before a risky bulk import).
* `POST /api/v1/admin/tenants/{tenant_id}/restores` — `{backup_id, mode: dry_run|promote, incident_ref}`.
* `GET  /api/v1/admin/restores/{restore_id}` — workflow progress and validation findings.
* `DELETE /api/v1/admin/backups/{backup_id}` — refused while `legal_hold` is true.

Events: publishes `TenantBackupCompleted`, `TenantBackupFailed`, `TenantRestoreCompleted`, `TenantBackupDestroyed`; consumes `TenantKeyShredded` (marks affected backups `destroyed` — the ciphertext survives but is provably unreadable, which is the point) and `TenantOffboarded`.

OpenFGA:

```
type tenant_backup
  relations
    define tenant: [tenant]
    define viewer: sre from platform or admin from tenant
    define restorer: sre from platform
    define promoter: sre from platform and incident_commander from platform
    define destroyer: sre from platform and dpo from tenant
```

Promotion and destruction both require an intersection of two distinct principals, encoding the two-person rule in the model rather than in a code path someone can bypass.

Sequencing: hard dependency on #30 (TEK must exist before any artefact is encrypted) and on #29 (prefix layout). Depends on the RLS data-access layer for the tenant-filtered dump. Issue #32's adversarial suite should be extended to cover restore artefacts. Issue #33 consumes `TenantBackupFailed` as a tenant-health signal.

Risks. (1) *A tenant-filtered logical dump is not transactionally consistent across tables if taken naively* — mitigated by a single repeatable-read snapshot for the whole dump and by recording the LSN, with the restore validating referential integrity before any promotion. (2) *Backup volume growth* — mitigated by tier-driven retention, incremental backups keyed on LSN, and a size-per-tenant metric feeding capacity planning. (3) *Restore of a tenant that has since had schema migrations applied* — mitigated by recording the schema version in the catalogue and refusing promotion when the backup's schema version is older than the live one without an explicit migration path. (4) *The restore path becomes a cross-tenant escape hatch* — mitigated because restore targets an isolated scratch cluster, promotion writes go through the same tenant-scoped data layer, and every restore is audited.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** an enterprise-tier tenant with an active TEK and 40 GB of clinical data
**When** the scheduled `TenantBackupWorkflow` runs
**Then** a full backup is written under `backups/IN/{tenant_id}/{backup_id}/`, encrypted under the tenant's current TEK version, a `tenant_backup` row is recorded with per-domain row counts and checksum, `TenantBackupCompleted` is published, and a dry-run restore of that artefact into a scratch database reproduces the recorded row counts exactly.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** a restore has been requested for tenant A and the operator supplies a `backup_id` belonging to tenant B
**When** `POST /api/v1/admin/tenants/{A}/restores` is called
**Then** the request is rejected with `422` and code `BACKUP_TENANT_MISMATCH`, no scratch database is provisioned, no decrypt is attempted against tenant A's key, and a `cross_tenant_restore_denied` audit record is written naming the operator, both tenant ids and the incident reference.

### Edge Cases

* A backup runs while a Temporal-orchestrated discharge workflow is mid-flight — the dump captures the repeatable-read snapshot, and restore validation flags the workflow as in-flight rather than restoring an inconsistent partial discharge.
* The tenant's TEK rotates between backup and restore — the artefact records `key_version` and is unwrapped against the retired version, which remains available for unwrap.
* `TenantKeyShredded` arrives for a tenant with 90 days of retained backups — every affected catalogue row moves to `destroyed`, the artefacts are deleted, and a single attestation covers the set.
* A backup is due for expiry while `legal_hold` is set (an ongoing DPDP grievance or a CERT-In-reportable incident) — expiry is skipped, and the hold and its reason are visible in the catalogue.
* Two on-demand backups are requested for the same tenant within a minute — the workflow ID `backup-{tenant_id}-{lsn}` deduplicates, and the second call returns the in-flight `backup_id`.
* Object storage returns a partial listing during manifest capture — the workflow retries the listing activity and fails the backup rather than recording an incomplete manifest that would silently lose attachments on restore.

---

## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.

### Accessibility and User Journey

### Documentation

* [ ] Known limitations are recorded.

---

## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** any single tenant can be restored to a defined point in time without affecting any other tenant, and every retained backup carries a dated verification record.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** RPO/RTO becomes a contractual commitment the platform can evidence; tenant offboarding and DPDP erasure extend cleanly into backups; NABH and tenant audits can be answered with verification records rather than policy text.
* **Success metric or validation method:** enterprise-tier RPO of 15 minutes and RTO of 2 hours demonstrated on a 40 GB tenant in a rehearsal, with restored per-domain row counts matching the manifest to 100%; at least 95% of tenants hold a verified backup no older than their tier's RPO on any given day; weekly automated restore verification covers a rotating sample such that every tenant is verified at least once per quarter, with zero unverified backups older than 90 days.
* **Monitoring period:** 90 days, tracking `tenant_backup_age_seconds` against tier RPO, `backup_verification_failed_total` (must remain 0), restore duration percentiles and backup bytes per tenant in OpenTelemetry.
