items.title: Replace the outbound denylist with an allowlist of permitted destinations on hosted deployments
items.body:
Raised in a partner's code review: *"For hosted deployments an allowlist of outbound destinations is a better model than a denylist of private ranges."*

This is the structural half of that review note. The rest of it — resolve and pin the IP, re-check on every hop, `redirect: "manual"` — patches the denylist. This replaces it.

## Why the denylist keeps losing

The guard in #2163 enumerates what to block: loopback, RFC1918, link-local, IPv6 unique-local, the platform-internal suffixes. Every entry is correct. The defect is the shape, not the entries:

- An IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal bypassed it, because the URL parser normalised the input into a form the unwrap never saw.
- The partner names DNS rebinding and `127.0.0.1.nip.io` as the next two, and both work for the same reason: the denylist reasons about the string, and the attacker controls the resolution.
- The `fc*`/`fd*` prefix match is already a false-positive class, so the list is simultaneously too permissive and too strict.

Each fix teaches the denylist one more encoding. There is no version of that list that is finished, because the input space is adversarial and the resolver is not ours.

An allowlist inverts the default. An unrecognised destination fails closed, so a novel encoding produces a refusal rather than a request, and the guard stops depending on having anticipated the attacker's spelling.

## What it would cover

The caller-supplied outbound fetch sinks, currently six: subscription webhook delivery, submission mirrors, peer registration, peer health probes, peer conflict resolution, and outbound sync webhooks.

## The real cost, stated plainly

A denylist is permissive by default and therefore invisible when it is wrong. An allowlist is restrictive by default and therefore **visible** when it is wrong — someone's legitimate webhook stops working and they have to ask. That is a support burden and a configuration surface, and it is the honest reason denylists get chosen.

Which means this is a hosted-deployment posture, not a global one. A self-hosted single-user install pointing a webhook at its own loopback should keep working without configuring anything, exactly as it does today. On a hosted multi-tenant instance the tradeoff reverses: the caller is not the operator, and outbound destinations are few and knowable.

## Open questions worth settling before building

- **Granularity.** Host, host plus scheme, or full origin? Full origin is tightest and the most annoying to configure.
- **Who administers it.** Instance operator only, or can a tenant add their own destinations within their own scope? The second is more useful and reopens the question this issue exists to close.
- **Migration.** An instance with existing subscriptions cannot switch to deny-by-default without breaking them. Needs a report-only mode that logs what *would* have been refused, run long enough to build the initial list from real traffic.

## Relationship to the other guard issues

Deliberately not a replacement for them. #2163 and #2164 should still land: the denylist is what protects instances until this exists, and it protects self-hosted installs afterwards. #2257 changes when the guard applies; this changes what the guard decides.

## Acceptance

- On a hosted deployment, an outbound fetch to a destination not on the allowlist is refused, whatever its encoding.
- A report-only mode exists and has been run against real traffic before enforcement is switched on.
- Self-hosted loopback behaviour is unchanged.

## Related

- #2163 / #2164 — the denylist guard this would eventually supersede on hosted deployments
- #2257 — gate the guard on public exposure rather than an opt-in flag

<!-- swarm-spec:start -->
## Swarm specification

_This section is maintained by the Ateles swarm. Each lens agent owns exactly one subsection below; the human-written description above these markers is never modified._

### Product / Scope (PM)

**Problem.** Six caller-supplied outbound fetch sinks (subscription webhook delivery, submission mirrors, peer registration, peer health probes, peer conflict resolution, outbound sync webhooks) currently rely on a denylist that is structurally unfinishable — every encoding fix teaches it one more spelling. On hosted multi-tenant deployments, invert to fail-closed: an allowlist of permitted destinations.

### In scope
- Allowlist-based enforcement on hosted deployments for the six named sinks (verified against #2164's sink inventory — accurate and complete as of this writing).
- A report-only mode: logs what *would* be refused without blocking, run against real traffic before enforcement switches on.
- Self-hosted/single-tenant behavior unchanged (loopback webhooks keep working with zero configuration).
- The three open design questions (host/origin granularity, operator-only vs. tenant-scoped administration, migration mechanics) — **resolution owned by arch (waxwing)**, not by this PM section. PM's steer: default to the tighter (full-origin) and more restrictive (operator-administered) option unless arch identifies a concrete cost that outweighs the security posture; loosen deliberately, not by default.

### Out of scope
- Removing or weakening the existing denylist (#2163/#2164 land and stay in force — protects instances pre-cutover and self-hosted installs permanently).
- Changing *when* the guard applies — that's #2257 (bind-posture-derived enforcement), sequenced independently.
- Tenant self-service destination management as a default behavior (explicitly flagged as reopening the original problem — defer to an explicit follow-up if arch/operator wants it).

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] On a hosted deployment, an outbound fetch to a destination not on the allowlist is refused, regardless of encoding (IPv4-mapped IPv6, DNS rebinding, `nip.io`-style resolution tricks, etc. — the class of bypass that motivated this issue).
- [ ] A report-only mode exists, has been run against real production traffic, and its output seeded the initial allowlist before enforcement is switched on.
- [ ] Self-hosted/loopback behavior is unchanged and requires zero new configuration.
- [ ] All six named sinks enforce identically — no sink left on the old denylist-only path after cutover.
- [ ] **Effect-verified fix**: tests assert the actual refusal behavior (blocked request never reaches the destination) for each encoding class in the acceptance bullet above — not merely that the allowlist config is accepted/validated.
- [ ] **Cross-surface parity**: each of the six sinks is tested independently, driven via its own natural call shape (webhook delivery via subscription flow, mirror via entity_submission flow, peer probes via sync flow, etc.) — a pass on one sink is not evidence for another.

### Priority & sequencing
- Land after #2163/#2164 (denylist hardening) merge — this supersedes them on hosted deployments but does not block their landing, and they remain the live protection until this ships.
- Independent of #2257 (posture-gating) — no ordering dependency either direction; both can proceed in parallel once each clears its own arch review.
- Recommended next: arch (waxwing) resolves granularity/administration/migration design, since those are unresolved architectural decisions this PM section deliberately did not settle.

### Confidence: high
Key assumption: the six-sink inventory in the issue body is current and complete. Verified against #2164's independently-audited sink list (matches exactly) as of 2026-08-28; if new outbound-fetch call sites are added before this ships, arch should re-confirm the inventory at implementation time.

### Open questions (for arch, not blocking pm sign-off)
- Granularity: host, host+scheme, or full origin?
- Administration: operator-only, or tenant-scoped within tenant's own boundary?
- Migration: how long must report-only run, and what's the promotion criteria from report-only to enforced?

### Engineering

**Mode:** spec authoring (`eng` lens). No gate verification, no PR, no code in this section.

#### Layering

Introduce a new layer that sits in front of the existing denylist guard from #2163/#2164, not inside it:

```
outbound fetch call site
  → OutboundDestinationGuard.check(url)
      1. resolve deployment posture (hosted vs self-hosted) — reuse #2257's posture signal if landed, else existing hosted-deployment config flag
      2. if self-hosted: delegate to existing denylist guard (unchanged path)
      3. if hosted:
         a. resolve+pin IP (same resolution step #2257/denylist patch introduces — reused here, not reimplemented)
         b. normalize destination key per configured granularity (host | host+scheme | origin)
         c. look up allowlist_entry for (tenant_scope, destination_key)
         d. mode = enforce → allow only on match, else refuse
            mode = report_only → always allow, but log a would_refuse event when no match
```

The allowlist guard wraps/precedes the denylist guard rather than replacing its code — denylist stays live for self-hosted and as defense-in-depth on hosted until confidence is high. Do not delete denylist logic in this PR.

#### Files/modules to touch

- `src/security/outbound_guard/denylist_guard.{ts}` (from #2163/#2164) — no logic changes; export its resolve+pin+re-check-per-hop helper so the new guard can reuse it instead of duplicating resolution logic.
- `src/security/outbound_guard/allowlist_guard.ts` (new) — implements the check above: `checkOutboundDestination(url, { tenantId, sinkName }): Promise<GuardDecision>`, where `GuardDecision = { allowed: boolean, mode: 'enforce'|'report_only', matchedEntry?: AllowlistEntry, wouldRefuse?: boolean }`.
- `src/security/outbound_guard/allowlist_store.ts` (new) — CRUD over the allowlist entries (see contract below); operator-scoped writes only per PM's default steer.
- `src/security/outbound_guard/deployment_posture.ts` — reuse/extend existing posture resolver (shared with #2257) rather than adding a second flag; if #2257 hasn't landed yet, add a minimal `isHostedDeployment()` here behind the same config key #2257 is expected to consume, so the two don't diverge.
- Six call sites to route through the new guard instead of calling the denylist guard directly:
  - `src/subscriptions/webhook_delivery.ts` (subscription webhook delivery)
  - `src/submissions/mirror_dispatch.ts` (submission mirrors)
  - `src/peers/peer_registration.ts` (peer registration)
  - `src/peers/peer_health_probe.ts` (peer health probes)
  - `src/peers/peer_conflict_resolution.ts` (peer conflict resolution)
  - `src/sync/outbound_sync_webhook.ts` (outbound sync webhooks)
  - (Confirm exact paths against #2164's sink inventory at build time — PM flagged this as the one assumption to re-verify.)
- `src/admin/allowlist_admin_routes.ts` (new) — operator-facing CRUD endpoints (REST) for allowlist entries; mirror whatever admin-route pattern the repo already uses for other operator-only config (e.g. denylist config route from #2163 if one exists).
- `src/cli/allowlist_cli.ts` (new, if repo has a CLI surface for admin ops) — same CRUD via CLI, for parity with any existing denylist CLI commands.
- `src/observability/would_refuse_log.ts` (new or extend existing structured logger) — emits report-only "would have refused" events with destination, sink, tenant, timestamp.

#### Data / contract changes

- New entity/table `outbound_allowlist_entry`:
  - `id`, `tenant_scope` (nullable = instance-wide; PM defaults to operator-administered, so tenant-scoped rows are schema-ready but not exposed via any tenant-facing API in this PR), `destination_key` (normalized per granularity), `granularity` (`host`|`host_scheme`|`origin` — pick one **instance-wide** setting per arch's resolution; do not support mixed granularity per entry in v1), `sink_scope` (nullable = applies to all six sinks; optional narrowing per sink if arch's granularity answer wants it — default null/all), `created_by`, `created_at`, `notes`.
  - Deployment posture config: extend existing hosted-deployment config (shared with #2257) with `outbound_guard_mode: 'denylist_only' | 'report_only' | 'enforce'`. Default `denylist_only` (today's behavior) until an instance explicitly opts into `report_only`.
- `GuardDecision` contract (internal, not persisted) as above — used uniformly by all six call sites so cross-surface parity is structural, not per-sink reimplementation.
- No breaking change to existing denylist config shape.

#### Build-step checklist

1. Land posture resolver reuse/stub (`deployment_posture.ts`) — coordinate with #2257 so there's one posture source of truth, not two.
2. Add `outbound_allowlist_entry` schema/migration + `allowlist_store.ts` CRUD.
3. Implement `allowlist_guard.ts`: resolve+pin+re-check (reusing denylist's helper), normalize by granularity, match against store, branch on `outbound_guard_mode`.
4. Implement `would_refuse_log.ts` structured logging for report-only mode.
5. Add operator admin routes (+ CLI if applicable) for allowlist CRUD, gated to operator identity only.
6. Migrate each of the six call sites, one at a time, to call `allowlist_guard.checkOutboundDestination(...)` ahead of (or wrapping) the existing denylist call — denylist call stays in place unconditionally as defense-in-depth.
7. Effect tests per sink (six total) driven via each sink's natural call path, asserting: (a) allowed destination reaches a stub/mock endpoint, (b) non-allowlisted destination in `enforce` mode never reaches the destination (assert on the outbound transport mock, not just guard return value), (c) `report_only` mode still delivers but emits a `would_refuse` log event for the same non-allowlisted destination.
8. Bypass-class regression tests (reuse #2163/#2164's encoding test fixtures): IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal, DNS-rebinding target, `*.nip.io`-style resolution — assert refusal in `enforce` mode for all three, on at least one sink (webhook delivery) plus a shared unit test at the guard level (not sink-duplicated) since the resolution logic is shared.
9. Self-hosted regression test: loopback webhook on a self-hosted-posture instance continues to succeed with zero allowlist configuration (denylist-only path).
10. Regenerate any generated artifacts touched (API/CLI schema docs, capability manifest, test catalog) as the last step before PR.
11. Document `outbound_guard_mode` states and promotion path (denylist_only → report_only → enforce) in operator-facing config docs; do not build a report-only "auto-promote" mechanism in this PR — promotion is a manual operator action informed by the would-refuse log, per PM's migration framing.

#### Explicit non-goals for this PR (deferred per PM/arch)

- Tenant self-service allowlist management UI/API.
- Auto-generating the initial allowlist from report-only log output (operator reads the log and populates entries manually in v1; tooling to semi-automate this is a reasonable fast-follow but out of scope here).
- Removing denylist code paths.

### QA / Test Plan

**Mode:** spec authoring (`qa` lens). Evals named here are the DoD for the impl PR — not yet runnable (no code). `gate_status.qa` stays **pending** until these are committed and green.

#### Surface under test (agent-first)

| Surface | Agent-observable effect |
|---|---|
| `checkOutboundDestination` (`allowlist_guard.ts`) | `GuardDecision` shape; refuse vs allow vs `wouldRefuse` |
| Six outbound sinks (eng inventory; re-confirm vs #2164 at build) | Transport mock: request reaches destination **or never** |
| `outbound_guard_mode` (`denylist_only` \| `report_only` \| `enforce`) | Mode branches above |
| Deployment posture (hosted vs self-hosted) | Self-hosted ignores allowlist; hosted applies it |
| Operator admin CRUD (`allowlist_admin_routes` + CLI if present) | Create/list/update/delete entries; non-operator denied |
| Agent MCP `subscribe` (webhook delivery sink) | Hosted+enforce: non-allowlisted `webhook_url` fails closed |

Foundation conventions loaded from `~/repos/foundation/conventions/testing_conventions.md` — mock only the outbound transport / DNS resolver; assert real guard + store behaviour.

#### Named evals (commit with impl PR)

| Eval id | Path | Asserts |
|---|---|---|
| `outbound_allowlist_guard` | `tests/unit/outbound_allowlist_guard.test.ts` | Shared guard: normalize+match; `enforce` refuse on miss; `report_only` allow + `wouldRefuse:true`; `denylist_only` delegates; bypass encodings (IPv4-mapped IPv6, DNS-rebinding target, `*.nip.io`) refuse under `enforce` **before** transport |
| `outbound_allowlist_sinks` | `tests/integration/outbound_allowlist_sinks.test.ts` | **Per-sink** effect matrix (below) — assert on `fetch`/transport mock call count, not only `GuardDecision` |
| `outbound_allowlist_admin` | `tests/integration/outbound_allowlist_admin.test.ts` | Operator CRUD contract on `outbound_allowlist_entry`; non-operator → 403/unauthorized; invalid `destination_key` / unknown granularity → 4xx; delete removes match so subsequent `enforce` refuses |
| `outbound_allowlist_hosted_enforce` | `packages/eval-harness/scenarios/outbound_allowlist_hosted_enforce.scenario.yaml` | Agent drives `subscribe` with non-allowlisted webhook under hosted+`enforce` → tool error / refusal; no delivery attempt. Companion happy path: allowlisted origin succeeds and returns `webhook_secret` (parity with `subscribe_webhook_secret`) |

Reuse #2163/#2164 encoding fixtures inside `outbound_allowlist_guard` — do not duplicate per sink.

#### Per-sink effect matrix (`outbound_allowlist_sinks`)

Each sink driven via **its natural call path** (PM cross-surface parity). For every sink, three cases:

| Case | Mode / posture | Assert |
|---|---|---|
| **S-allow** | hosted + `enforce` + entry present | transport mock **called** once with expected URL |
| **S-refuse** | hosted + `enforce` + no entry | transport mock **never called**; sink returns typed refusal (not a transport timeout) |
| **S-report** | hosted + `report_only` + no entry | transport mock **called**; structured `would_refuse` log emitted with `{destination, sink, tenant, timestamp}` |

Sinks (fail the suite if any one is missing its describe block):

1. subscription webhook delivery
2. submission mirrors
3. peer registration
4. peer health probes
5. peer conflict resolution
6. outbound sync webhooks

#### Regression / edge cases (must appear as named `it(...)`s)

- **Bypass class (guard + webhook sink):** IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal; DNS rebinding (resolve flips to private between check and connect — pin+re-check path); `127.0.0.1.nip.io`-style hostname — all refuse under hosted+`enforce`.
- **Self-hosted loopback:** posture=self-hosted, zero allowlist rows, webhook to `http://127.0.0.1` / `localhost` **succeeds** (denylist-only path; allowlist not consulted).
- **Default mode:** fresh config `outbound_guard_mode=denylist_only` behaves as today (no allowlist refusals on hosted until explicitly promoted).
- **Defense-in-depth:** hosted+`enforce`+allowlisted destination that is still private-range → denylist still blocks (allowlist wrap does not bypass denylist).
- **Granularity mismatch:** entry stored under configured granularity; URL that matches host but not origin (if granularity=`origin`) refuses.
- **`sink_scope`:** entry scoped to sink A does not admit sink B under `enforce`.
- **Idempotent refuse:** duplicate outbound attempts to the same non-allowlisted URL refuse identically (no partial delivery).
- **Empty / malformed URL:** guard refuses closed; transport never called.
- **Tenant scope (schema-ready):** instance-wide entry (`tenant_scope=null`) matches; no tenant-facing write API in v1 — assert tenant credentials cannot mutate allowlist (`outbound_allowlist_admin`).

#### Contract tests — admin endpoints

- `POST/GET/PATCH/DELETE` (or repo-idiomatic equivalents) for allowlist entries: 2xx + persisted `outbound_allowlist_entry` fields (`destination_key`, `granularity`, `sink_scope`, `tenant_scope`, `created_by`).
- Authz: operator identity only; anonymous / tenant / non-operator → 401/403.
- CLI parity (if `allowlist_cli` ships): same CRUD outcomes as REST for create + list + delete.

#### Explicit non-coverage (recorded)

- Auto-promote report_only → enforce (out of scope).
- Tenant self-service allowlist UI/API (out of scope).
- Production “ran report-only against real traffic” acceptance bullet — **operator runbook / release checklist**, not a CI eval; CI asserts the **logging contract** (`would_refuse` event shape) only.

#### Acceptance checklist (qa lens)

- [ ] `outbound_allowlist_guard` green — bypass encodings refuse under `enforce`; modes branch correctly
- [ ] `outbound_allowlist_sinks` green — all **six** sinks have S-allow / S-refuse / S-report; refuse asserts `fetch` call count `=== 0`
- [ ] `outbound_allowlist_admin` green — operator CRUD + non-operator denied
- [ ] `outbound_allowlist_hosted_enforce` scenario green in eval-harness / `agentic_evals` lane
- [ ] Self-hosted loopback regression green with empty allowlist
- [ ] Denylist path still invoked on hosted (defense-in-depth case green)
- [ ] Test catalog / generated artifacts regenerated if the repo requires it
- [ ] No silent skip of a sink: inventory count asserted (`expect(coveredSinks).toHaveLength(6)` or equivalent)

**Sign-off rule:** APPROVE / `gate_status.qa=signed_off` only when the four named evals are in the PR and CI-green — or a recorded `no functional surface` judgement (N/A here; this is functional).

### Security / Arch

Comment posted. Closing the turn with the assistant-message bookkeeping store (already done above in the combined call — that satisfies step 5a/5b).

## 🧠 Neotoma — [Issue #2258](https://neotoma.markmhendrickson.com/inspector/conversations/ent_52e1136654cd35a4e33ffc2f)

**Created (2)**
- 🏛️ [plan_contribution](https://neotoma.markmhendrickson.com/inspector/entities/ent_6158e502763c8631a9c88ec1) — Waxwing arch review, `blocking: true`
- 💬 [conversation_message](https://neotoma.markmhendrickson.com/inspector/entities/ent_958d63933e977ce3ef497d15) — assistant turn (arch verdict)

**Retrieved (2)**
- 💬 [conversation](https://neotoma.markmhendrickson.com/inspector/entities/ent_52e1136654cd35a4e33ffc2f) — Issue #2258 thread
- 💬 [conversation_message](https://neotoma.markmhendrickson.com/inspector/entities/ent_19fd5d65d6105991b8429c70) — Pavo's prior pm sign-off

---

## Summary

I wrote and posted the **Security / Arch** section for #2258 (issue body updated via the `<<<SPEC_SECTION>>>` fence above — the dispatcher will merge it in). Key resolutions:

1. **Granularity → `host`** for v1 (config-driven, `origin` schema-ready for later tightening).
2. **Administration → operator-only**; `tenant_scope` stays schema-present but write-inert — no tenant write path, ever, without a fresh ADR.
3. **Migration → no auto-promote, standing constraint** — report-only log is operator-readable evidence only, never a write trigger.

Plus hard gate requirements: contract-first ordering (schema/`GuardDecision` before sink migration), tenant isolation on every lookup, `idempotency_key` on all admin mutating ops (REST + CLI parity), credential-exposure constraints on the would-refuse log (no full URLs/secrets, local-first telemetry posture), and defense-in-depth ordering (denylist always still runs after allowlist match).

**Verdict: REQUEST_CHANGES** — one blocking gap: eng's build-step checklist doesn't yet direct an update to the MCP/CLI agent-instruction surfaces (`tool_descriptions.yaml`, `instructions.md`, `cli_agent_instructions.md`) to tell agents about the new `subscribe` destination-refusal mode. Everything else is guidance for implementation, not a blocker. Posted as a GitHub comment (not the spec body) per the swarm contract, with the ADR backlinked to the Neotoma conversation entity.

### Legal

### Legal / Compliance

**Mode:** spec authoring (`legal` lens). Risk analysis, not legal advice. Jurisdiction: Spain (EU) · regimes GDPR, ePrivacy, Spanish commercial law (`locale_profile` `ent_ea9a413189860f872c6cc99a`). Project licence: **MIT** (`product_profile:Neotoma` `ent_73226bffbccbd1ff7ff04e49`).

Builds on PM/Eng/QA/Arch: operator-only admin, host granularity v1, no auto-promote, credential-minimized `would_refuse` log, denylist defense-in-depth.

#### Dependencies / licensing
- [ ] Any new npm/pip deps are MIT / Apache-2.0 / BSD-2/3 / ISC — **no** GPL, AGPL, SSPL, CC-NC, or other copyleft/commercial-restrictive licences
- [ ] Prefer zero new deps (compose on existing outbound-guard modules from #2163/#2164)
- [ ] Vendored third-party code (if any) ships with LICENSE + required attribution

#### PII / data-handling (public-effect + telemetry)
Calibrated to GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) minimization and Art. 32; aligns with arch credential-exposure constraints:
- [ ] `would_refuse` events log **only** normalized `destination_key` (or host), `sink`, `tenant_scope` id, timestamp, mode — **never** full URLs, query strings, fragments, `Authorization` headers, `webhook_secret`, guest tokens, or request/response bodies
- [ ] Report-only and enforce paths must not dump destination payloads (entity bodies, subscription event content) into the would_refuse / observability path
- [ ] Would-refuse retention is bounded (existing local-first log retention or explicit TTL) — not a permanent PII store; no cross-border telemetry export of raw destinations without a separate review
- [ ] Agent / MCP / CLI refuse errors are a typed “destination not permitted” (or equivalent) — **must not** enumerate allowlist entries, other tenants’ destinations, or internal `outbound_guard_mode` to guest callers
- [ ] Denylist still runs after allowlist match (defense-in-depth) — reduces unauthorized access / SSRF exposure to personal data

#### Guest-token / credential scope
- [ ] Allowlist admin CRUD: **operator identity only**; guest tokens, tenant API keys, and anonymous callers → 401/403 (non-waivable; QA already asserts)
- [ ] Guest `subscribe` / the six outbound sinks gain **no** allowlist read or write capability via any new route
- [ ] Successful `subscribe` returns `webhook_secret` only to the authenticated creator; refuse path must not return, rotate, or log secrets
- [ ] Peer-sync / `guest_access_token` flows: allowlist enforcement must not broaden token scope or leak cross-tenant `destination_key`s in error bodies
- [ ] `tenant_scope` schema-ready but write-inert (arch) — **legal concurs**; tenant self-service reopens the SSRF control gap this issue closes — requires a fresh ADR **and** legal re-review before any write path

#### ToS / operator disclosure
- [ ] Operator docs for `outbound_guard_mode` (`denylist_only` → `report_only` → `enforce`) MUST state that `enforce` may break previously working destinations not on the allowlist — no silent cutover
- [ ] Self-hosted / loopback posture remains zero new configuration (no new ops burden on single-tenant installs)
- [ ] No public marketing / claims surface in this change set

#### Escalation
- No qualified-counsel escalation for this PR (not a contract above EUR 10k threshold; not IP dispute / employment / regulatory enforcement matter).
- Re-escalate if: tenant self-service allowlist is proposed; would_refuse logs are exported off-instance; or public claims about compliance guarantees are added to marketing copy.

**Legal verdict on spec:** APPROVE — no `[BLOCKING]` legal items. Arch’s agent-instruction coherence gap remains Waxwing’s blocker, not a legal gate hold.
<!-- swarm-spec:end -->

items.title: Live-data cutover map — mock fixture → Supabase rows
items.body:
## Destination

The TVI-CAMS app renders the dashboard slice from **live Supabase rows** instead of the `unconfigured` mock fallback, with `shared/mocks/seed.ts` transformed into schema-shaped seed data that coexists with whatever real rows the project already holds.

Reaching the end of this map means: the target Supabase project is awake and connected, every mock entity has a decided mapping onto the migration schema (or a decided verdict of "not seeded" / "derived" / "needs a column"), and the seed is a reviewed artifact ready to apply. **Charting only** — this map decides the mapping; applying it and rewriting the `data/` layers is downstream work.

**Assumption to confirm in [Lock the destination — seed the DB, or finish the mappers?](<https://linear.app/tesda-cams/issue/TES-83/lock-the-destination-seed-the-db-or-finish-the-mappers>) (first grilling ticket):** "map my mock data to match my supabase schema" is read as *transform the fixture into rows that fit the schema*, not *finish the DB-row → UI mappers* (those run the other direction and largely exist already).

## Notes

* Domain: TVI-CAMS / TESDA-CAMS multi-tenant TESDA scholarship compliance tool. Governing docs in precedence order per `CLAUDE.md`: `docs/adr/ADR-001-billing-and-domain-model.md` (+ ADR-003) > `docs/TRD.md` > `docs/MASTER_PRD_SRS.md`.
* **Grounding facts established while charting (2026-08-23):**
  * Supabase project `tesda-compliance-manager` (ref `azywaivpyphhsblxjgtn`, ap-northeast-2) is **INACTIVE / paused** — `list_tables` times out. Two adjacent ACTIVE projects exist (`tesda-cbc-agent`, `tesda-cbc-agent-dev`); the target must be confirmed before anyone restores anything.
  * `.env.local` holds **Clerk vars only — no Supabase vars at all**. Every existing `data/` contract therefore takes the `unconfigured` branch and silently serves mocks on every request. This, not the mappers, is why "real data" has never appeared.
  * The DB is **not pristine**: `supabase/migrations/20260717054607_migrate_akb_tenant_and_drop_rogue_table.sql` migrated real AKB tenant rows out of a rogue camelCase `public.tenant` table. Expect `tenants.code = 'AKB'` to already exist and collide with `unique (code)`.
* **Mock fixture inventory** (`shared/mocks/seed.ts`, 503 lines): 3 tenants (AKB / J3ED / NEN), 9 users across all 5 roles, 3 batches (BAT-1/2/3, 47 scholars total), 12 `DOCUMENT_REQUIREMENTS` keys, plus `ACTIVITY`, `ALERTS_LOG`, `SNAPSHOTS` and heavy enrichment passes.
* Scope boundary vs shuakyle21/tesda-compliance-manager#28 (`Complete data contracts in module data/ layers`, High, In Progress, flipped back to In Progress today): shuakyle21/tesda-compliance-manager#28 owns the `modules/*/data/` fetch→map→derive contracts and its AC line "Seed data committed and consistent with migration seed." This map owns getting correct rows into the live DB and the app connected to it; shuakyle21/tesda-compliance-manager#28 **owns the contract layer.** Do not create tickets here that duplicate shuakyle21/tesda-compliance-manager#28's remaining scope (`learners.ts`, `lamr.ts`, `activity.ts`, `attendance.ts`, `metrics.ts`).
* Scope boundary vs shuakyle21/tesda-compliance-manager#116 (LAMR data-contract map): LAMR schema shape and its `program_modules` decision belong there, not here.
* Skills to consult per ticket: `grilling` + `domain-modeling` (wayfinder default), plus `supabase` and `frontend-layered-architecture`.
* **Standing constraint (rule 36 / project memory** `supabase_execution_permission`): never run `execute_sql`, `apply_migration`, or branch operations against the live project without the user's explicit yes. Restoring the paused project and applying any seed are therefore HITL `task` tickets, never agent steps.

## Decisions so far

* [Confirm the target Supabase project and restore it from paused](<https://linear.app/tesda-cams/issue/TES-84/confirm-the-target-supabase-project-and-restore-it-from-paused>): target is `tesda-compliance-manager`, ref `azywaivpyphhsblxjgtn`, URL `https://azywaivpyphhsblxjgtn.supabase.co` — user-confirmed, now `ACTIVE_HEALTHY`. All 3 migrations applied, RLS on all 15 public tables. Free tier, so it re-pauses after ~1 week idle.
* [TES-88 identity strategy, batches only](<https://linear.app/tesda-cams/issue/TES-88/identity-strategy-mock-string-ids-tnt-akb-bat-1-uuid-primary-keys>) (2026-08-31): batch identity = the RQM code parsed from the batch's NTP (e.g. `RQM3-2026-CFSP-1263-0009`), stored as `batches.batch_code`, natural-key-upserted against `unique (tenant_id, batch_code)`. Tenant identity stays separate (`tenants.code`). Surfaces a new gap: no RQM-code parsing/validation pipeline exists yet — manual entry only, until a document-parsing feature is scoped.

## Not yet specified

* The ~20 `shared/types.ts` `Batch` **fields with no schema home** — `trainingDays`, `trainingDaySchedule`, `duration`, `currentDay`, `totalDays`, `ntpLag`, `tipDate`, `aouDate`/`ntpDate`, `bsrs`, `competencies`, `scheduleAdjustments`, `egace`, `employmentFollowUp`, `scholars_list`, `hoursPerDay`, … Each needs a *derive / new column / drop from UI* verdict. Several tickets' worth once the frontier reaches it; deliberately not pre-sliced.
* Whether `ACTIVITY`, `ALERTS_LOG`, `SNAPSHOTS` and attendance get seeded at all, or stay mock-only until their features are real.
* Seed mechanics and re-runnability — one-shot SQL vs idempotent upsert script, where it lives in the repo, and how it interacts with the existing migration seed block.
* How the dashboard's `?role=` / `?state=` preview overrides behave once rows are real (touches shuakyle21/tesda-compliance-manager#32's tenant/role resolver).

## Out of scope

* The future Express.js/Node backend — documented direction only; explicitly do not scaffold or pre-empt it (`CLAUDE.md`, project memory).
* Any `modules/*/ui` work — this map produces data and decisions, not screens.
* The unmigrated remainder of ADR-001 §11 (`attendance_records`, `batch_trainer_assignments`, `scholarship_cost_schedule`, `billing_records`, `tenant_settings`, `learner_identities`) — future maps.

items.title: Migrating Substantial app to Apartments
items.body:
This is more of a question/advice than it is an actual issue.  We really like this gem, we think it's awesome.  We have a monolithic app which lends itself naturally to apartmentalization.  There are essentially two top level objects, a company, and a user.  The company is relationally attached to all the related objects as the top of the tree via active record relations (i.e. we can traverse down all items owned by a particular company), and we will want to apartmentalize our application for the company as we want data separation between companies that our application manages.

Given that apartment seems like a really attactive solution to us, I was hoping to get some answers to some questions:
- Has anybody done this?  Essentially pried apart their app into apartments.  Would be really nice to know if there's any specific gotchas!
- Is there any helpful gem or tools anybody has used to "move house"?  Essentially help the process of migrating from one apartment to many apartments.  We'd have to do it piecemail as a single migration to do this would likely lead to far too much downtime for our customers.
- Who out there is using Apartment to do data separation in a larger application... am I understanding freshbooks uses it?  Any really noteable pitfalls as you scale with this solution?
- Looks like the authors really intended this for Postgres, we are on MySQL (RDS).  Anything majorly wrong with apartmentalization on MySQL?

Thanks for any help and advice you might give!

-Bramski (payrollhero.com)

items.title: Backend phase 1 — program brief (NestJS multi-tenant server, Architecture A + T1)
items.body:
> **This is the program brief, not a unit of work.** It covers the NestJS backend for the Srisurart POS, **phase 1 only** — the server, its database, its CI, and the demo-tenant delivery. Phase 1 of Architecture C is by definition Architecture A + tenancy model T1, and every ADR treats them as identical. Phase 2 (offline shell, outbox, sync) and the Flutter `ApiRepository` client layer are separate specs.
>
> **The implementable work is split into child issues**, one per seam in the dependency chain that `handoff/grill-round2-ci.md` and `03_ARCHITECTURE.md §8` already draw. Those carry the `ready-for-agent` label; this brief does not. Read this for the invariants and acceptance criteria, then pick up a child issue.
>
> Synthesised from the backend design package in `docs/Backend_design/` (docs 00–04 + ADR-0001…0011), the two `handoff/` records, the course rule summaries, and the Dart repositories that are the behavioural reference. **Where this spec and an ADR disagree, the ADR wins.**
>
> Everything cited here is committed as of `f6c082a`, including the round-3 QA section, the faculty-VM quota, and the confirmation that the VM accepts inbound connections.

## Child issues

Dependency order. The foundation is a single chain nobody can parallelise; the three lanes then run together. **Split into vertical slices on 2026-09-05** — the four lane/foundation issues below are now parents holding shared context, and the grabbable work is in their children.

- [ ] #12 — counter-facing Thai wording for three error codes *(blocks #4, #6)*
- [ ] #13 — confirm the pos-only endpoint list *(blocks #6, #24, #28)*

**Foundation — the chain**
- [x] #3 — `p1`+`p2` foundation *(parent)*
  - [x] #14 — `p1` compose stack, Nginx, health probes

**Lane C — cache, rate limit, queues, export, k6** *(unassigned)* · #9 *(parent)*

- [ ] #32 — `p8.2` invalidate-after-commit across every write path
